# Abre

**Nonprofit helps city build capacity for collective intelligence projects**

- Category: CI How-to
- Topic: Urban Green Space
- Location: Peñalolén, Chile
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: Fundación Ciudadanía Inteligente
- Years in operation: 2017 - present
- Platforms: Web; in-person
- Project website: https://abre.tumunicipio.org/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

[Abre](https://abre.tumunicipio.org/) is a platform and method for cities to engage their community in the creation, design, implementation, and evaluation of a local project through a mixture of online and offline consultation. Fundación Ciudadanía Inteligente (FCI or Smart Citizenship), a Chilean non-profit that works on democratization projects in over 10 locations across Latin America, is the creator of Abre, a four-step process for engaging residents in the co-design of city services. Peñalolén, a city with 250,000 inhabitants in the Santiago Metropolitan Region of Chile, collaborated in the design of Abre and piloted its use in 2017, when 200 citizens submitted more than 40 proposals to redesign the city’s San Luis Park. While Abre is one of many examples of cities co-creating services with citizens, Abre is notable for its focus on capacity-building within the city government.

**Background:**

Abre was co-designed by the Fundación Ciudadanía Inteligente and city officials from Peñalolén in 2017. FCI was looking to develop a new initiative that would apply the foundation’s expertise in civic technology to a real-world local government project. Peñalolén, meanwhile, wanted to create greater opportunities for its citizens to participate using new technology. The organization and city formed a partnership to design and test FCI’s four-stage engagement methodology (Proposals, Design, Implementation, and Evaluation) by redesigning the city’s central park, Parque San Luis, with input from the surrounding community.

Prior to the start of the project, FCI developed a website ([penalolen.tumunicipio.org](http://web.archive.org/web/20190212130740/https://penalolen.tumunicipio.org/)), based on the open-source [Consul](http://consulproject.org/en/) platform. Consul is a toolkit for citizen engagement, originally developed in Spain, and in use in over 100 communities around the world. The website hosted the online portions of the initiative, namely the proposal and voting phases. FCI then hosted two training sessions in which the Abre process was explained in detail to working groups within the city’s government.[1] They then engaged local leaders and those in the surrounding area in a four week long campaign to get the word out and encourage participation.

**The result?**

One result of the pilot was the creation of a new design for Parque San Luis. The final design included elements like new paving, more trees, a community garden, a dog park, and new lighting. The necessary funding for the remodelling process was awarded by the regional government in 2019, and work began on the new park in the same year. The [political crisis](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2019/dec/17/chile-mental-health-protests-uncertainty) in Chile further delayed the park’s completion, but the city expects to open the new park in March of 2020.[2]

Another key result was capacity building within the City of Peñalolén. Smart Citizenship transferred ownership of the [penalolen.tumunicipio.org](http://web.archive.org/web/20190212130740/https://penalolen.tumunicipio.org/) website to Peñalolén after the online portions concluded. The website is now hosted on the city’s servers. While there are no active challenges on the site, it could be used to repeat the Abre process independent of FCI in the future. The City did just that in 2018, with the Ciudadano Medioambiental (“Environmental Citizens”) challenge, where local schools proposed ideas for environmental projects that could be developed on vacant lots in Peñalolén.

Although a change in leadership and a loss of funding at FCI ended its involvement in Abre Peñalolén, FCI is planning to re-launch Abre through a school for public servants of local governments of Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Mexico in 2020.

**How it Worked:**

Proposal - The first stage was conducted online using the Abre platform. The platform was open for citizens to submit proposals about what features they would like to see in the new park, and to vote on the proposals of others. A mixed team of FCI members and city employees conducted offline outreach, liaising with community members and offering them access to computers to create their proposals.

Voting - Over the course of a month, citizens submitted over 40 proposals and cast more than 200 votes of support. The three proposals that received the most votes then advanced to the design stage.

Design - During the Design phase, the city hosted a series of workshops to work out a design for the park. Those who lived in the community surrounding the park were invited to attend two co-design sessions, where the municipality presented the three "winning" proposals, which were used as the starting point for the design process. Those two sessions produced a plan that synthesized the inputs from citizens into one balanced and feasible project.

After the first two stages, ownership over Abre Peñalolén transferred from FCI to the City of Peñalolén.

The latter two stages --implementing the chosen plan and evaluating the result with input from the community-- were left to the city. In the end, the public did not participate in implementing the plan because the city delivered the project through a contract that did not allow for third parties to be involved. As the new park includes a dog park, once the park is open the city will organize training on responsible ownership of pets to keep the community involved in the project. [3]

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/cbfaac2e-3521-4ebd-82a1-224634985898.png)*

*Figure 1: The four-stage Abre methodology (Source:* [*https://abre.tumunicipio.org/*](https://abre.tumunicipio.org/)*)*

**Why it Worked:**

1. **Clear Ownership:** The Abre Peñalolén project clearly allocated ownership based on which aspects of the project each partner could deliver. While FCI was tasked with designing the methodology, creating training materials, and developing the website the initiative used, the city was able to define the problem it wanted solved and retained ownership over the final design and its implementation. Crucially, ownership over the penalolen.tumunicipio.org website was transferred to the city following the completion of the first two phases of the project. Despite FCI pulling out of the project, the transfer of ownership means that Peñalolén can still deliver the project on its own, and also has the digital infrastructure for a similar collaborative design project in the future.
2. **Collaborative Design:** Manuel Barros, one of the former leaders of the project, emphasized in an interview that Abre’s success was in large part due to the fact that it was designed in collaboration with the city officials. There was political will at a government level. In addition, the project worked effectively in campaigning with local leaders.[4]

## End notes

1. “CrowdLaw Speaker Series: Manuel Barros, Abre,” The GovLab, June 24, 2018, video, [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-DMmAlZcmF8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-DMmAlZcmF8).
2. Cecilia Jiménez, email, 14 January 2020
3. Cecilia Jiménez, email, 14 January 2020
4. Manuel Barros, interview, 4 December 2019.

id: "collective-intelligence:case/propeller-health"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "AIR Louisville / Propeller Health"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/propeller-health"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "Using GPS-enabled inhalers, the Louisville Metro Government tracked asthma/COPD incidents and decreased rescue inhaler use by 82% among equipped participants"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# AIR Louisville / Propeller Health

**Using GPS-enabled inhalers, the Louisville Metro Government tracked asthma/COPD incidents and decreased rescue inhaler use by 82% among equipped participants**

- Category: Problem Solved
- Topic: Public Health
- Location: United States
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: Louisville Metro Government / Propeller Health
- Years in operation: 2012-present / 2010-present
- Platforms: Mobile app
- Project website: https://www.airlouisville.com/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) can be pervasive, impairing, expensive, and even life-threatening, especially when patients do not receive proper treatment. In the United States asthma is a prevalent condition - 7.6% of people over 18 years of age have it and 13.6 % have had it at some point.[1] Apart from the health implications, these conditions cost the US economy over $80B per year, according to research published in the Annals of the American Thoracic Society.[2] The study found that, for the 15.4M people in the US with treated asthma, the associated out-of-pocket medical cost of asthma each year was $3,266 per person.  **To address the serious challenge of asthma, the city of Louisville**, **Kentucky, a city where poor air quality makes it one of the “most challenging” in the US for people with asthma to live, turned to the collective intelligence of its residents to get more timely and objective data of where and when asthma is occurring.[3]**

A key problem in effective and rapid treatment -- and prevention -- is accurate and complete information about the onset of an incident. Doctors are reliant on patients’ ability to recall factors surrounding an incident and patients may not be aware of contributing environmental factors. At a health research and policy level, the typical method for studying asthma outbreaks in specific locations is to conduct inefficient personal interviews with each patient, which could take months or even years.

Confronted with this problem in Louisville was Ted Smith, the Louisville Metro Government’s Chief of Civic Innovation. Smith says he knew that Louisville:

> ...had a very high rate of breathing disorders compared to the national average. I spent enough time with companies having a hard time relocating to Louisville because of this, that when Mayor Fischer asked me what was on my innovation agenda, I knew this had to be part of it.[4]

Smith saw an opportunity to “revolutionize” asthma treatment in collaboration with the digital health firm, [Propeller Health](https://www.propellerhealth.com/) (then a research project called Asthmapolis) and local partners.[5] In 2012, they launched the [Air Louisville](https://www.airlouisville.com/index.html) pilot program to capture better data about asthma and COPD triggers so they could use the knowledge to inform better interventions. Support from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation enabled participation in the program to be expanded to include hundreds more residents.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/06182644-9133-44f5-bf7e-d0d02b796239.png)*

*Figure 1: A Propeller Health inhaler fitted with sensors (Source:* [*https://www.airlouisville.com/about.html*](https://www.airlouisville.com/about.html)*)*

**The result?**

In Air Louisville, 1,147 residents signed up to Propeller Health’s mobile app and were given inhalers fitted with sensors.

The sensors captured data on the location, date and time, and dosages of inhaler use.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/f58a950b-bb1e-47ba-bc01-36bb72e79b87.jpg)*

*Figure 2: Image of the asthma risk “heat map” (Source:* [*https://www.airlouisville.com/results.html*](https://www.airlouisville.com/results.html)*)*

The platform combines this data with air quality and weather data to create a map of triggers for asthma and COPD incidents across the city. The app also enables patients to get reminders to self-medicate and other tips for managing their condition.

**Using the map of asthma and COPD triggers, the Metro Government identified steps it could take to improve air quality. This included developing recommended routes that directed trucks away from at risk neighborhoods, planting more trees, and considering zoning policies that create buffer zones around schools and residential areas to minimise the effect of highways and industrial emissions.** The Government also introduced a notification system to alert residents when poor air quality and weather conditions increased the risk of incidents.[6] Ted Smith, now a Professor of Environmental Medicine at the University of Louisville, meets regularly with Metro Government staff to discuss further implementation of the recommendations.

**Over a period of 12 months, the Air Louisville program observed in participants enrolled in the project:[7]**

- **An average of 82% reduction in asthma rescue inhaler use**
- **29% of uncontrolled participants gained control of their asthma**
- **On average, participants more than doubled their symptom-free days**
- **Participants slept better, with an average 19% increase in symptom-free nights.**

Air Louisville data continues to be applied in other ways. It was used to show health improvements after two energy plants switched from coal to natural gas. It has also helped to launch a new project led by the University ofLouisville - [Green Heart](https://greenheartlouisville.com/) - a five-year clinical trial in which researchers are examining whether increasing green space in a neighborhood improves air quality and human health.

Adoption of Propeller Health’s technology has grown too. Propellor’s sensors and app are now used by more than 100,000 people in the US for managing asthma or COPD.[8]  As of 2017, Properllor’s technologies were deployed in more than 45 programs, some of which include large health systems such as [Dignity Health](https://www.dignityhealth.org/).[9] The Propeller mobile app also continues to evolve and now includes a feature that helps people to manage their prescriptions and find a local pharmacy.

**How did it work?**

Air Louisville began with a pilot study conducted by the Metro Government and Propeller Health (then-known as Asthmapolis) in 2012, with 300 inhaler sensors distributed to Louisville residents. This pilot helped to demonstrate that, contrary to popular belief, asthma triggers were not specific to where the participants lived but rather appeared all over the place due to different environmental factors.[10]

The pilot generated significant public interest, including from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, which supported Ted Smith and the Community Foundation of Louisville to create the Institute for Healthy Air, Water and Soil. A partnership involving the Institute, the Mayor’s office, Louisville Metro Government, Propellor, and a coalition of employers, healthcare providers and advocacy groups that helped to enroll participants in the program, then developed and launched the expanded version of Air Louisville.  A total of 1.2 million data points were collected, including 251,000 medication puffs, that were combined with over 5.4 million environmental data points to create the map of asthma and COPD triggers that informed the Louisville Metro Government’s responses.[11]

Propeller Health’s app and sensors gather and share data by:[12]

- Distributing inhalers fitted with sensors to asthma and COPD patients and signing patients up to the Propeller app to track inhaler usage
- Storing the data captured In a central cloud that enables it to be aggregated, sorted and shared back with patients, doctors, researchers and policy makers
- Using the app to share back with patients information about their inhaler use, including visualizations, reports, reminders and a forecast based on the environmental factors of a location on a given day
- Providing doctors access to a web portal where, with patient permission, they can monitor a patient’s progress, adherence to medication, and state of asthma control
- Sending alerts to a patient’s doctor when a patient misses controller use for four consecutive days or is at risk of an exacerbation of their condition.

**Why It Worked**

The success of Air Louisville can be attributed to:

1. **Data sharing that enabled collective action:** By combining existing data sources with new data collected by patients and sharing it in useful ways, Air Louisville helped to develop a trusted evidence base for targeted interventions by government and patients themselves.
2. **Strategic partnerships**: By partnering with Propeller Health the government gained access to an existing suite of digital health products while collaboration with employers, healthcare providers and advocacy groups built participation in the program as well as the legitimacy of it.
3. **User focus**: Propeller’s system accounted for the needs of patients who already confronted the challenge of managing a chronic condition and rather than assign patients more tasks, automated the data collection through the sensors and the app.
4. **Technology**: The advent of smartphones and cloud computing unlocked the potential of digital health generally, and in Air Louisville, was key to enabling resident participation and faster data collaboration at scale.
5. **Addressing an agreed, high priority problem**: There was consensus among key stakeholders that air quality and respiratory illness was a significant issue that needed to be addressed in Louisville.

## End notes

1. US Department of Health and Human Services, *Summary Health Statistics: National Health Interview Survey, 2018*, accessed February 16, 2020, [https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health\_Statistics/NCHS/NHIS/SHS/2018\_SHS\_Table\_A-2.pdf](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/NHIS/SHS/2018_SHS_Table_A-2.pdf).
2. American Thoracic Society, “Asthma Costs the US Economy More than $80 Million Per Year,” January 12, 2018, [https://www.thoracic.org/about/newsroom/press-releases/journal/2018/asthma-costs-the-us-economy-more-than-80-billion-per-year.php](https://www.thoracic.org/about/newsroom/press-releases/journal/2018/asthma-costs-the-us-economy-more-than-80-billion-per-year.php).

6. Gary J. Kurtzman, “A Breath of Fresh Air: An Oral History of Propeller Health,” *Safeguard* (blog), September 6, 2017, [https://www.safeguard.com/2017/09/06/breath-fresh-air-oral-history-propeller-health/](https://www.safeguard.com/2017/09/06/breath-fresh-air-oral-history-propeller-health/).

id: "collective-intelligence:case/civic-bridge"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "Civic Bridge"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/civic-bridge"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "By working with private sector technologists and designers, the City of San Francisco taps pro bono talent worth millions"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"

# Civic Bridge

**By working with private sector technologists and designers, the City of San Francisco taps pro bono talent worth millions**

- Category: Kind of Collaboration
- Topic: City Services
- Location: San Francisco, United States
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: City of San Francisco
- Years in operation: 2015 - present
- Platforms: In-person
- Project website: https://www.innovation.sfgov.org/civic-bridge
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

**Surrounded by Silicon Valley, San Francisco leaders saw a golden opportunity to improve the lives of residents by bringing private sector talent to bear on pressing City problems. Civic Bridge -- a 16-week program teaming up city staff and private sector experts to design better City services -- enables San Francisco to do just that.**

Civic Bridge unleashes the power of skilled volunteers to help solve San Francisco’s biggest problems. Early on the City hosted one-off “hack-a-thons” that generated a lot of good ideas.  But these sessions left city staff with no clear roadmap for implementation. In 2015, the Mayor’s Office created a volunteering program to help innovation generate real change. Civic Bridge brings the private sector and City departments together to co-create, design and implement improved City services. Today San Francisco’s [Office of Civic Innovation](https://www.innovation.sfgov.org/) (OCI), housed within San Francisco’s Department of Technology, runs the program.

Civic Bridge works with city agencies to select a problem to tackle -- such as improved access to affordable housing or better management of non-emergency 911 calls. OCI then recruits a cohort of volunteer technologists and designers from Bay Area tech companies. These volunteer experts spend the next four months with City staff collaborating on a solution.

While the experts and City team innovate, OCI provides guidance and helps to identify resources. Dee Prasad, Interim Director of OCI, says Civic Bridge helps to “facilitate the matches” between City departments and the private sector:

> “When \[the private sector\] went directly to a department they spent a lot of time trying to find a way to work together - and departments are busy. So we aim to do it in a more strategic way by asking ‘where do we know there is a need?’ and use our city-wide perspective such as the Mayor’s priorities as a guide.”[1]

**Companies looking for pro bono projects to inspire and reward employees connect with City departments in need of professional skills they can’t source in-house.** Companies find partnering with the City through a single entry point easier than one-time partnerships that must be constantly negotiated, and Civic Bridge’s organized and tested approach incentivizes companies to participate with the promise of well-scoped projects. In turn, City departments benefit from access to highly-skilled professionals whose contributions are relevant and reliable, with companies committed to releasing staff for 20 percent of their weekly working hours during the program.

One of the first issues tackled through Civic Bridge was improving the City’s application process for affordable housing. Originally, applicants had to apply with different forms for every public housing opportunity. This excessive paperwork created unnecessary stress for thousands of low-income residents. First, a Civic Bridge team of Google engineers and City staff went “secret shopping” and put themselves in the shoes of residents looking for housing to understand the problem. Then, using Google’s expertise in human-centered design, the team worked with residents to come up with a list of what a new, centralized, online portal would need to help residents apply more easily. This list included streamlined applicant requests, information storage and fewer forms. After a design phase, the City published a request for proposal to bring the portal to life. Today, 85 percent of applications are processed through this website, which requires residents to complete just one application form.

**The result?**

What started as a pilot program in 2015, has grown to include the work of 250 volunteers on 49 projects, sourcing an estimated $US 3.9 million in pro bono contributions. The 2019 cohort comprised nine teams working on things like improved transitional housing, more efficient street cleaning, and improved access to City services for transgender communities. Civic Bridge was also announced as a winner in the 2019 [Engaged Cities Awards](https://engagedcitiesaward.citiesofservice.org/), which is organized by the nonprofit Cities of Service to recognize cutting-edge techniques that engage residents to solve problems.

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/56a50c32-a583-436d-bbec-af469ec9a532.png)

*Figure 1: Screenshot from the Office of Civic Innovation website (Source:* [*https://www.innovation.sfgov.org/civic-bridge*](https://www.innovation.sfgov.org/civic-bridge)*)*

Krista Canellakis, former Chief Innovation Officer of San Francisco, explains that this type of co-design process can help transfer skills and interests between the public and private sectors.[2] City staff get to apply new learning to their work more broadly and private sector volunteers gain a new appreciation for the complexity of City problems, which can spur volunteers to give more time in support of civic good.

While larger companies sometimes have more resources and established infrastructure for pro bono partnerships, Civic Bridge is working on building ways for smaller companies to contribute. Canellakis is aware of this challenge, especially since working with larger companies with HR departments capable of coordinating volunteers can reduce work for the City. Employees of larger companies are also more likely to be allowed to take on pro bono commitments. Smaller start-ups sometimes struggle relinquishing employees for the 16-weeks needed for a project sprint. However, the City continues to grow Civic Bridge and is working to make its programs more accessible to different kinds of organizations. Recently, Civic Bridge introduced a “Day of Service” model, which identifies innovative tasks that can be addressed in a single day, making it easier for small companies to play a role.

**How does it work?**

City departments submit applications to OCI to be a part of an annual cohort. Projects that align with Mayoral and departmental priorities (where the department has committed resources for solutions to be implemented) are more likely to be chosen. OCI staff then prepare selected departments for external partnerships by helping them to map out an appropriate scope. OCI staff know sixteen weeks will go by more quickly than expected and also assist by gathering relevant data from around the City. OCI staff then market the project to company leaders to recruit volunteers.

After blended teams of four to eight people from the City and a company have been assembled, these groups spend six to ten hours per week working on their projects.  The first eight weeks are focused on understanding the problem, while the second half of the program is directed at designing solutions and preparing recommendations in consultation with departments. Kick-off and mid-program meetings with the entire cohort help generate momentum and keep projects on track. OCI staff also check in weekly with teams to monitor progress, help identify “low hanging fruit” for quick wins and guide implementation planning. Each team presents their work at a public event called “Demo Day” attended by the Mayor and program outcomes are shared widely on social media and via blog posts and newsletters.

After a cohort’s 16 weeks of collaboration is complete, OCI staff meet with City departments at 6 and 12 month intervals to assess a solution’s implementation and its impact. They also conduct surveys and publish insights about [project outcomes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1b6OT8u01smq0ZV_mtvF1juj9RZT-36rYKtglLcwl3jU/edit).

OCI structures Civic Bridge to create intimate, engaged teams that can steer meaningful work at different levels. A cohort of volunteer teams all start at the same time and project teams are kept small. OCI has a project manager assist teams and track progress, with a senior manager (half-time) to oversee corporate partnerships. Each team is also assigned a City executive to champion the work.

**Why It Works**

The success of Civic Bridge can be attributed to:

1. **An innovative business model**: By conceiving of companies as co-designers of solutions, rather than the city as ‘purchaser’ and company as ‘provider’, Civic Bridge acts as a platform for a new kind of value exchange that was previously unrealized.
2. **Structured support**: Substantial effort goes into project scoping to provide for a sense of accomplishment that motivates stakeholders and generates buy-in.
3. **Strong incentives to participate**: Pre-commitments by the City (such as Mayoral priority projects with allocated resources and pledged in-kind staff support from private companies for an extended timeframe) can make it an attractive program for both company staff and city departments to participate in compared with traditional volunteer programs.
4. **Efficient delivery**: OCI’s project guidebooks include templates for projects and setting clear expectations, as well as the necessary forms and standard emails that make it quick to set up new projects.
5. **Strategic alignment**: Projects are consistent with Mayoral priorities which supports buy-in throughout the city administration.

## End notes

1. Dee Prasad, City of San Francisco, Interview, November 26, 2019.
2. Interview, Krista Canellakis, formerly of City of San Francisco, Interview, October 27, 2019

id: "collective-intelligence:case/decidim-helsinki"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "Decidim Helsinki"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/decidim-helsinki"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "Helsinki uses participatory budgeting to enable public engagement in urban policymaking"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# Decidim Helsinki

**Helsinki uses participatory budgeting to enable public engagement in urban policymaking**

- Category: Task Performed
- Topic: City Development
- Location: Helsinki, Finland
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: City of Helsinki
- Years in operation: 2018-2019
- Platforms: Decidim; in-person
- Project website: https://omastadi.hel.fi/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

Since participatory budgeting (PB) was first introduced in the City of Porto Alegre, Brazil in 1989, hundreds of cities around the world have allocated a portion of their budget through citizen deliberation. Helsinki began the first trial of its citywide participatory budgeting program in 2018. Helsinki’s approach combined online proposal creation and voting, using the [Decidim](https://decidim.org/) platform, with an offline strategy for outreach and deliberation. Anyone could propose small-scale projects that fell within the city’s jurisdiction, while residents of Helsinki age 12 and over were eligible to vote on which to implement. Over the course of a month, participants submitted 1,273 proposals for how to allocate a budget of €4.4 million towards small-scale projects within their neighborhoods. At the end of the process in October of 2019, the city approved 44 project plans for implementation. **While many cities use participatory budgeting, some with budgets vastly exceeding that of Helsinki, the Finnish capital is a useful example of how to use PB both to prioritize capital improvements but also to foster civic engagement. The City went to great lengths to engage with residents and make PB a highly participatory and collaborative process. The model has been so successful that, after an initial pilot the City has formalized the use of PB as a regular part of city life.**

**Background**

Upon taking office in 2017, Helsinki’s mayor and city council began a series of structural changes to make the city’s government more responsive to the public. Participatory budgeting was implemented in Helsinki in 2018 as part of this larger overhaul.

To ready the city for the participatory budgeting process, the City Council made a decision to split the funds between seven boroughs. Over a one month period, residents could propose ideas online for projects either at the city level or that fell within the borough in which they lived. Further, the city hired seven “borough liaisons”-- civil servants hired to increase civic participation within their neighborhoods and provide information about PB. As part of the offline outreach effort, the city worked with a local design firm to develop a card game to help users understand the PB  process and come up with ideas for projects. The game centers around six different kinds of playing cards, each corresponding to one aspect of the PB process (e.g. limiting factors, citizen personas, city districts) tailored to spark conversation among players and help them develop ideas for funding. The card game was played by hundreds of people at workshops where physical (and [digital](https://omastadi.hel.fi/uploads/decidim/attachment/file/15/OmaStadiplaycards_.pdf)) copies were also distributed for free.[1]

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/7406ef14-7b49-4fd5-87a6-970bd9665f66.png)

*Figure 1: The OmaStadi Participation Game (Source:* [*https://medium.com/@BloombergCities/how-a-card-game-can-help-city-residents-suggest-new-ideas-b1da60bb112b*](https://medium.com/@BloombergCities/how-a-card-game-can-help-city-residents-suggest-new-ideas-b1da60bb112b) *)*

“The game is a tool to make \[Participatory Budgeting\] approachable,” Kirsi Verkka, Development Manager at the City of Helsinki, told Bloomberg Cities. “Not something that feels complex or bureaucratic, but something where you can sit down with people, have a good time, and do something for your community.”[2]

The online portion of the PB process was conducted on [OmaStadi.hel.fi](https://omastadi.hel.fi/). This website uses Decidim based on the Consul framework, a free and open source citizen engagement platform used by numerous city and regional governments and non-profit organizations.

**The Result**

The PB trial run, which began in 2018 and lasted through 2019 produced 1,273 ideas for funding, which over the course of a year were adapted into 296 project plans that were put to a vote. At the end of voting, the city approved 44 projects for implementation.[3] The list of project plans and those approved for each district were published on the initiative’s [results page](https://omastadi.hel.fi/pages/aanestystulokset?=). The winners ranged from a €120,000 plan to install more trees, benches, and trash cans throughout the city to a €50,000 plan to build a new basketball court in a central suburb.

**Based on the success of the first round, the participatory budgeting process will now be formally included as part of the regular municipal budgeting process. “In general I hope this has raised awareness among the people to participate in talks about what happens in the city,” Kirsi Verkka told a local media outlet. “The essence of the whole project was that we would have an open discussion with citizens.”[4]**

The city government also collected demographic data on votes to assess how votes varied by age, gender, and region. The city government sent out a survey to all the participants via email to which approximately 300 people responded. In an interview Katja Hentonnen, one of the leaders of the PB project, described the responses as positive overall, but did note that one of the most common complaints was that the budgeting process benefited wealthy areas, with many of the winning projects going to already wealthy regions.[5]

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/f4f8e197-befc-415e-915e-f2c7840c6706.png)

*Figure 2: The OmaStadi website (Source:* [*OmaStadi.hel.fi*](https://omastadi.hel.fi/)*)*

**How it Worked**

The participatory budgeting process was run over the course of a year through six steps:[6]

1. Citizens generated ideas at brainstorming workshops led by borough liaisons
2. Citizens uploaded ideas to OmaStadi.hel.fi; city officials from the relevant departments commented on and evaluated ideas against eligibility criteria
3. Borough liaisons and city-level coordinators transformed ideas into plans through co-creation workshops,
4. City departments created budget estimates for each plan
5. Citizens voted on the plan they wish to see implemented
6. Plans are now being executed by the relevant city departments

In May of 2018, the borough liaisons hosted a seminar to kick-off the participatory budgeting process. While some citizens attended in person, many others joined an online livestream, where they could comment on the proceedings in real-time, with comments shown on a large screen at the center of the stage. This event set the tone for the combined online-offline approach that would characterize the rest of the initiative.

In October and November of 2018, the public generated ideas for what to fund. Borough liaisons hosted a series of workshops where they explained the PB process, distributed the aforementioned card game, and answered questions about how to submit ideas on OmaStadi.hel.fi. The website was open for submission between mid-November and mid-December, during which time residents submitted 1,273 ideas. This included a range of proposals from improving the infrastructure of local parks, to creating new street art, to designing a scenic walking route through Helsinki. At the same time, representatives from the city’s divisions evaluated each idea against the city’s eligibility criteria. Each idea that was eliminated received a comment explaining why (e.g. it was not within the city’s jurisdiction to build). This resulted in 839 approved ideas.

From January - April, 2019, city officials and residents transformed eligible ideas into implementable plans that could be cost-estimated. This was done through a series of in-person workshops where citizens collaborated with borough liaisons to create a plan either out of a single idea or by combining similar ideas. Again, citizens then uploaded these plans to OmaStadi.hel.fi, where citizens and city officials could comment on them. City divisions were then responsible for preparing a cost estimate for each plan.

During the month of October, residents could vote on the plans that fell within one district of their choice or that were to be implemented at the city level. Any resident of Helsinki age 12 or older could vote online, or during events held at local libraries and community centers. For those aged 12 to 17, the platform also included a separate youth participatory budgeting project section called “Ruuti Budget” in which young people could raise ideas for development of youth and leisure services. The youth contingent was allotted €330,000 to allocate to youth-related activities.

In the pilot, a total of €4.4 million was available for funding, with one-fifth of this amount reserved for city-wide plans. The remaining pool of funding was divided between the seven boroughs. The winning projects were determined through a rolling system, where the top-scoring plan in each borough received funding. Funding was then allocated to the next highest-scoring plan that did not exceed the remaining budget, and so on until no plans remained.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/c86712d2-fd29-488d-a947-41d11fa274ec.png)*

*Figure 3: A visualization of the funding allocation process for a sample area (Source:* [*https://omastadi.hel.fi/uploads/decidim/attachment/file/1927/%C3%84%C3%A4nestystulos\_visualisointi\_alusta\_english.pdf*](https://omastadi.hel.fi/uploads/decidim/attachment/file/1927/%C3%84%C3%A4nestystulos_visualisointi_alusta_english.pdf) / [*CC BY-SA 4.0*](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/legalcode)*)*

**Why It Worked**

The success in the trial run of Decidim Helsinki can be attributed to:

1. **Clear Opportunities to Participate:** The city made good use of public resources such as libraries, community centers, and schools to reach participants. Other novel offline approaches, such as the card game played at ideation workshops, created an enthusiastic pool of participants with a clear idea about how to engage. The offline outreach process provided residents with a clear understanding of how to engage, leading to a large volume of participation. Hentonnen, for instance, told the story of her own son’s kindergarten class emailing the parents to urge them to participate.
2. **Learning From Experience:** Katja Hentonnen shared that based on the post-project survey results, the team identified usability as a key issue. As such, the team is working on improving their use of the Decidim platform for the next round of participatory budgeting.

## End notes

2. “How a Card Game Can Help City Residents Suggest New Ideas,” *Medium* (blog), *Bloomberg Cities*, March 13, 2019, [https://medium.com/@BloombergCities/how-a-card-game-can-help-city-residents-suggest-new-ideas-b1da60bb112b](https://medium.com/@BloombergCities/how-a-card-game-can-help-city-residents-suggest-new-ideas-b1da60bb112b).
3. “Participatory Budgeting Makes Your Ideas and Voice Heard,” OmaStadi, City of Helsinki, accessed February 17, 2020, [https://omastadi.hel.fi/](https://omastadi.hel.fi/).

Petja Pirhonen, “Power to the People: Helsinki Divides Up More than €4 Million on Citizen Projects,” *News Now Finland*, November 1, 2019, [https://newsnowfinland.fi/domestic/power-to-the-people-helsinki-divides-up-more-than-e4-million-on-citizen-projects](https://newsnowfinland.fi/domestic/power-to-the-people-helsinki-divides-up-more-than-e4-million-on-citizen-projects).

id: "collective-intelligence:case/flint-property-portal"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "Flint Neighborhood Inventory / Flint Property Portal"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/flint-property-portal"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "Data crowdsourced from residents helps Flint secure $US67.5 million to restore blighted neighborhoods"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"

# Flint Neighborhood Inventory / Flint Property Portal

**Data crowdsourced from residents helps Flint secure $US67.5 million to restore blighted neighborhoods**

- Category: Problem Solved
- Topic: Housing
- Location: Flint, Michigan, United States
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: Genesee County Land Bank Authority and the City of Flint
- Years in operation: 2012-present / 2017-present
- Platforms: Website; Mobile app
- Project website: https://flintpropertyportal.com
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

From its peak in 1960, the City of Flint’s population fell by more than 50% by 2018, leaving the city with many vacant homes and empty or unsafe lots. Approximately 21,500 of Flint’s properties, representing 38% of all properties in the city, were considered blighted. Blighted properties are those that are so dilapidated and unsafe that they impede economic growth.[1] Residents identified access to property information and addressing blight as one of their top priorities but local authorities did not have the resources or data to respond effectively.

In 2012, the Genesee County Land Bank Authority - a government organization that manages tax-foreclosed properties - the City of Flint, and the Community Foundation of Greater Flint, partnered to create the Flint Neighborhood Inventory Project. The project involved 27 community-based groups that surveyed the condition of properties in their neighborhoods, enabling the City to obtain existing condition data for a large part of the city and to build relationships with these groups, laying the foundation for a subsequent master planning

community engagement. In turn, that engagement process led to the development of the [Flint Property Portal](https://flintpropertyportal.com/).

Launched in 2017, the Portal displays property data collected by the Land Bank and the City and complements that with data collected from residents. Through the Portal website and mobile app residents can add to the information about a property’s condition. The CIty encourages resident contributions through an annual Neighborhood Inventory program and the Land Bank does the same through a [Clean & Green program](http://www.thelandbank.org/clean_green_prog.asp) that involves the public in maintaining vacant lots. The Portal’s “Maintenance Message” function also enables residents to report their community work, such as boarding, trash removal, and mowing. The City and the Land Bank then use the Portal data to help them make decisions about properties and public services from water pipe replacement to building permits and urban planning.

On the Portal website, residents can also create maps that depict the condition of properties in specific areas or even city-wide, offering them an up-to-date and transparent picture of property conditions.

**Before the Flint Neighborhood Inventory and Flint Property Portal projects, the City and the Land Bank had limited information about blighted properties but using the collective intelligence and collective action of its residents, the Land Bank and the City have created a detailed picture of blight in the city and made it easily accessible to the public.**

**The result?** Through the first Neighborhood Inventory in 2012, residents completed a citywide census of all 56,000 properties in Flint, so that the City and the Land Bank could determine the scale of blight issue and where the specific problems were. The Land Bank, in partnership with the City, then used the data to identify properties in need of demolition as part of a successful application to the US Treasury Hardest Hit Fund that awarded $US67.5 million in blight elimination grants for the Flint area. These grant funds have been used to demolish more than 4,500 blighted structures.[2] In total, users have submitted more than 250,000 messages through the Portal. Of those, 165,000 are from groups participating in the Your Neighborhood Inventory and Clean & Green programs and a further 10,000 are from the general public. The remainder are contributions made by the Land Bank and City staff.

**Perhaps most important, this collaboration between government and citizens has given everyone a transparent picture of conditions in their own city and empowered residents through the process of collaboration in problem-solving.**

Christina Kelly, Director of Planning and Neighborhood Revitalization, Genesee County Land Bank Authority, explains:

Now, more than ever, we need to be transparent. \[The Genesee County Land Bank Authority\] believes the Portal is an effective way to maintain transparency between government and citizens. The stronger the trust between the two, the better they will be able to work together.[3]

**How does it work?**

Consisting of a website and a mobile app, the portal collects, combines and displays 60 points of data for each of Flint’s 56,000 properties. The CIty and the Land Bank selected these data points in response to both the public’s interest and their own data uses.

The Portal offers three main functions:

- Property Lookup: Within the Portal exists a “profile” for every property in the city of Flint, which includes a photograph and up to 40 pieces of property specific information. Anyone with internet access can view this information by entering an address or parcel number or by selecting it using the online map. Residents can easily find out who owns a property, if it is vacant, if it is on a demolition list, and, if it is owned by the Land Bank, when it will be demolished.
- Property Update: Users can report property condition changes through the Property Update feature to keep local officials informed. After selecting a property by inputting the address or parcel number, users can report these changes. All of this information is viewable to the public in a “property feed.” In the app, users are asked to select a land parcel and answer three questions: “What is the property condition?”; “Is the building occupied”; and “Is a blight visit needed?” Then they can upload a photo of the property and add any accompanying text they wish in a text box.
- Map Making: The Portal gives users the ability to map property information. Users can choose to view maps from a list of categories such as demolition status, property condition, and future land use, or they can create their own map using nearly 30 criteria for any area within Flint, small or large.

Through a [partnership](http://www.thelandbank.org/downloads/FlintPropertyPortalCaseStudywGraphics.pdf) between the Community Foundation of Greater Flint and the City of Flint, a Your Neighborhood Inventory initiative is conducted annually to help community groups assess the condition of properties in their neighborhoods. The City identifies inventory needs and engages with participating groups on data collection and improvement plans while The Community Foundation of Greater Flint selects participating groups through an application process and awards a $500 mini-grant to each group that is accepted. The Land Bank’s Clean & Green program similarly involves community groups in maintaining vacant lots and posting maintenance messages and property condition updates to the Portal.

To support the introduction of the Portal, the City and the Land Bank hosted three open house workshops to train people in using the Portal and to get feedback on its design. The cost of developing the Portal totaled approximately $US 220,000.

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/0d9a9abb-ca44-43e5-9798-cc3a58c631bf.png)

*Figure 1: Screenshot of the city map with the “property condition” filter selected.” Areas of red indicate “sub-standard.” (Source:* [*https://flintpropertyportal.com/*](https://flintpropertyportal.com/)*)*

**Why it Works**

1. **Transparency:** Residents are involved in both collecting and using the data, and any resident can search the data on the Flint Property Portal. As a result it has become a trusted source of information. Developed mainly as a response to the public’s demand for more information, the Portal gives residents straightforward and clear access to public data that they didn’t previously have.
2. **Currency of data:** The Portal makes up-to-date data held by the Land Bank and the City available and easy to use and understand for the public, and provides citizens the opportunity to update the information at any time. The City also updates its data that’s linked to the Portal on a monthly basis, so all datasets and information on the Portal are timely, allowing accurate information to be collected and shared to inform and prioritize effective property remediation.
3. **Community engagement**: The Land Bank and the City have long built a community around the Portal, presenting it to residents and asking for feedback before it was launched in 2017. After listening and revising the Portal based on that feedback, the Land Bank and the City launched the Portal with a series of community launch events held throughout Flint. Afterwards, Land Bank and City staff continued to attend community meetings to share information on the Portal and help residents learn how to download and use the app and website.

## End notes

1. City of Flint, Michigan, *Annual Action Plan Program Year 2018/2019*, June 2018, [https://www.cityofflint.com/wp-content/uploads/Action-Plan-2018.pdf](https://www.cityofflint.com/wp-content/uploads/Action-Plan-2018.pdf).
2. “Flint, Michigan, Winner,” Engaged Cities Award, Cities of Service, accessed February 16, 2020, [https://engagedcitiesaward.citiesofservice.org/flint-michigan-2019-winner/](https://engagedcitiesaward.citiesofservice.org/flint-michigan-2019-winner/).
3. Christina Kelly (Genesee County Land Bank Authority), interview, November 14, 2019.

id: "collective-intelligence:case/ipaidabribe"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "iPaidABribe"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/ipaidabribe"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "An Indian nonprofit created a platform to enable public reporting of bribery and now crowdsources data from more than 1,000 cities"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# iPaidABribe

**An Indian nonprofit created a platform to enable public reporting of bribery and now crowdsources data from more than 1,000 cities**

- Category: Task Performed
- Topic: Anti-Corruption
- Location: India
- Implementation level: national
- Owner: Janaagraha Center for Citizenship and Democracy, Bengaluru
- Years in operation: 2010-present
- Platforms: www.ipaidabribe.com
- Project website: http://www.ipaidabribe.com/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

Corruption in government in India is believed to be rampant. A recent survey of 20,000 citizens across 20 Indian states by Transparency International found that 1 in 2 respondents said they had paid a bribe in the past year.[1] The widespread problem of small-scale corruption, sometimes referred to as “retail corruption,” negatively impacts citizens’ ability to avail themselves of government services such as obtaining a birth certificate or a drivers license, especially by those who can least afford to pay such bribes.[2] The Anti-Corruption Bureau and the Central Vigilance and Anti Corruption Office, the two federal government agencies responsible for investigating corruption, provide official channels to report corruption by email or phone, yet, instances of bribery are severely underreported by citizens out of a fear of retribution.[3]

To address the need for anonymous ways to report corruption and enable the public to obtain a more accurate picture of public officials demanding bribes, [ipaidabribe.com](http://www.ipaidabribe.com/) uses the power of the Web to crowdsource corruption reporting. The [Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy](http://www.janaagraha.org/), a Bengaluru-based nonprofit founded by Swati and Ramesh Ramanathan, created [iPaidABribe](http://ipaidabribe.com/en#gsc.tab=0) to quantify the extent of low-level corruption in India by providing people an anonymous, online mechanism to report their experiences of public corruption as well as positive experiences of interactions with honest public officials. **The goal is to “use the data to engage positively with any arm of the government to improve services and reduce the possibility of corruption.”[4]**

The iPaidABribe website enables people throughout India to report the nature, number, pattern, types, locations and frequency of corrupt acts. All the information is then presented publicly as maps and reports that can be filtered by location and government department. The aim is to provide anti-corruption activists and government officials with a crowdsourced repository of knowledge of the corruption that confronts citizens in their daily lives and which can be used to advocate for systemic change in service delivery.

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/bedb0d0f-7994-4cd4-83c5-b1f75ac10dd4.png)

*Figure 1: A data visualization of the top five departments in Mumbai where iPaidABribe users have reported experiences of bribery (Source:* [*http://www.ipaidabribe.com/bribe-trends/city/mumbai#gsc.tab=0*](http://www.ipaidabribe.com/bribe-trends/city/mumbai#gsc.tab=0)*)*

**The result?** Since its inception in 2010, 15 million platform users have reported 193,199 instances of corruption in 1,080 Indian cities, totaling an estimated monetary value of 34 billion Indian Rupees (approximately $US 479 million).

A few months following its launch in 2010, several hundred reports of corruption at the Regional Transport Offices (RTOs) in the South Indian state of Karnataka appeared on the website. RTOs are responsible for issuing drivers licenses and several users had expressed anguish at the bribes they had to pay in order to obtain their licence. **The activity on the platform, which was widely reported in local media and on the Internet, caught the attention of Transport commissioner Bhaskar Rao. At his invitation, Janagraaha presented a report of the crowdsourced complaints to RTO staff. Based on the evidence, the RTO took several steps to reduce opportunities for corruption. These included digitizing services and making the status of applications transparent. After a departmental inquiry, 20 officials were also suspended for taking bribes.[5]**

Similar process re-engineering informed by iPaidABribe data also helped to reduce the potential for [corruption related to registering land](http://www.janaagraha.org/i-paid-a-bribe/) for purchase or sale in Bengaluru. Before the change, government processes required attendance at a specific sub-registrar’s office depending on where the land parcel was located. Analysis of the data found a “flourishing market for bribes in land transactions” with offices on the periphery of the city, where most of the transactions occur, seeing the greatest rates of bribes.[6] Based on this, the Department of Stamps and Registration accepted an iPaidABribe proposal to enable land registrations at any office.

In December 2017, iPaidABribe won an International Anti-Corruption Excellence Award presented at the United Nations Office in Geneva in recognition of its innovation in anti-corruption. iPaidABribe has been replicated by several countries and is currently active in fifteen.

**How does it work?**

iPaidABribe is a publicly accessible website where people can report three things:

- Paying a bribe
- Standing up to corruption and refusing to pay a bribe, or
- Meeting an honest officer and not having to pay a bribe.

Upon selecting one of the three options, people then fill out a short form to describe their experience. The form asks for information, including the department and city in which the bribe was solicited, the reason, and the amount of money. The platform provides the option to stay anonymous or to report the incident to the relevant local anti corruption department (in which case they are required to provide their contact information). The portal compiles these user-generated reports into a [“corruption monitor”](http://ipaidabribe.com/bribe-trends#gsc.tab=0) and encourages media and government officials to scrutinize the data. To discourage spurious reports, the names of officials accused of bribery are anonymized.[7] Stories of success and honest officials are also shared through the portal.

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/8e97d7d5-76bb-48de-b0e3-2aba98da0e24.png)

*Figure 2: Screenshot depicting reports that people can make through the iPaidABribe website (Source:* [*ipaidabribe.com*](http://www.ipaidabribe.com/))

A “How-to” section of the website provides information about processes and procedures for commonly used public services to help people be aware of their rights and resist attempts at bribery. Services covered include obtaining a passport or birth certificate, school admission, building plan approval, trade licences, gas connection, railway trip planning, police complaints, paying income tax, and many more. An “Ask An Expert” function enables people to pose questions of former, senior public servants. The site also offers a link to a [legal service](https://www.lawfarm.in/) where people can have their initial legal questions answered online for free and if necessary get help in finding a lawyer.

Social media, search engines and news and research articles are used to promote the site and encourage the public to report their bribery experiences.

Currently, iPaidABribe is only accessible through a web browser on desktop and mobile and is only available in English and Hindi. To extend its usability, especially in India which has 22 official languages, Janagraaha is working towards including more Indian languages and creating a mobile interface - a medium which has grown rapidly in India in the past decade.

**Why It Works**

1. **Large pool of potential participants**: Low level corruption is a frequent problem experienced by many people in India which means that the portal can gather data at scale and direct responses to ‘hotpots’ or uncover patterns that warrant further investigation.
2. **Removal of a key barrier to participation**: The portal addresses the biggest risk potential contributors face - retribution from those they report - by allowing anonymized reports of bribery experiences.
3. **Simple data capture process**: The online forms are simple for participants to use and capture data in a consistent way that enables useful data visualizations and data insights to be created.
4. **Transparency and data sharing**: By publishing summary data on its public website, as well as sharing information with government authorities and media, iPaidABribe enables other stakeholders the opportunity to identify patterns of low level corruption that can be addressed through advocacy and changed procedure rather than through more costly and risky judicial processes alone.

## End notes

1. Transparency International India, *India Corruption Survey 2019: Bribery in India Reduced by 10% Over the Last 1 Years; 51% Citizens Admit to Paying a Bribe in the Last 12 Months,* [http://transparencyindia.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/India-Corruption-Survey-2019.-Press-Release.pdf](http://transparencyindia.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/India-Corruption-Survey-2019.-Press-Release.pdf).
2. Samuel Paul, “Corruption: Who Will Bell the Cat?” *Economic and Political Weekly* 32, no. 23 (June 1997): 1350-55, [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4405484?seq=1](https://www.jstor.org/stable/4405484?seq=1).
3. Shri Amrit M. Prasad, *Corruption - A Grossly Under Reported Crime*, 2011, [https://odishavigilance.gov.in/Odisha\_Vigilance/Pub%20File/Chapter-9.pdf](https://odishavigilance.gov.in/Odisha_Vigilance/Pub%20File/Chapter-9.pdf).
4. “Rajasthan,” I Paid a Bribe (website), accessed February 18, 2020, [http://ipaidabribe.com/#gsc.tab=0](http://ipaidabribe.com/#gsc.tab=0).
5. Mukti Jain Campion, “Bribery in India: A Website for Whistleblowers,” *BBC News*, June 6, 2011, [https://www.bbc.com/news/world-south-asia-13616123](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-south-asia-13616123).
6. “I Paid a Bribe,” Janaagraha (website), accessed February 18, 2020, [http://www.janaagraha.org/i-paid-a-bribe/](http://www.janaagraha.org/i-paid-a-bribe/).
7. id: "collective-intelligence:case/sustainable-neighborhoods-program"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "Sustainable Neighborhoods Program"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/sustainable-neighborhoods-program"
date: "2021-03"
summary: "Lakewood tapped residents’ passion for improving their neighborhoods to create a community-led sustainability ‘workforce’"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# Sustainable Neighborhoods Program

**Lakewood tapped residents’ passion for improving their neighborhoods to create a community-led sustainability ‘workforce’**

- Category: CI How-to
- Topic: Sustainability
- Location: Lakewood, Colorado, United States
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: City of Lakewood
- Years in operation: 2010 - present
- Platforms: sustainableneighborhoodnetwork.org website; In-person
- Project website: https://www.sustainableneighborhoodnetwork.org/sustainable-neighborhoods-lakewood
- Case study last updated: March 2021
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

When elected officials and city staff in Lakewood, Colorado, a mid-sized suburb of Denver, wanted to pursue sustainability goals, rather than relying on scarce city resources, they enlisted residents’ help and created a community-based sustainability “workforce.” **To help the City achieve its sustainability goals, the city has created a way for citizens to design, run and implement their own sustainability projects.**

Previously, the city worked with residents in the usual way through planning system processes that left people with little opportunity to contribute once decisions had been made. Typically, residents could come to a planning meeting to offer feedback about plans already-made or channel ideas through a part-time neighborhood planning officer but this left the planner overwhelmed and residents frustrated.

The city’s planner Jonathan Wachtel changed this by introducing the [Sustainable Neighborhoods Program](https://www.sustainableneighborhoodnetwork.org/sustainable-neighborhoods-lakewood) in 2010. The program encourages residents with passion, ideas, and know-how to propose projects that they will develop and implement with neighbors. **As Wachtel explains, he wanted to change how he worked because “a lot of people had interest and expertise...all the inquiries around green topics kept getting directed my way...I was getting tired of not being able to say anything except thank you.”** Given the libertarian and free-spirited culture of Colorado, the Mayor wanted to make sure that the project didn’t tell citizens what to do but, instead, allowed them to self-select to participate and design their own projects.

The city supports neighborhood projects with technical advice, leadership coaching, and help to secure grants and to navigate city bureaucracy. It is an approach that enables the city to invest in feasible and impactful proposals by working with enthusiastic residents on projects capable of making a significant contribution to the city’s sustainability goals. For example, residents in the neighborhood of Morse Park have a tree planting initiative with a goal to plant 200 new trees on private residential properties by the end of 2020. To date, 120 residents have planted 134 trees, which is contributing to the city’s target of 30 percent tree canopy coverage by 2025.[1] After the initial pilot in 2010, the full program was rolled out in 2012 and now includes eight neighborhoods covering 20 percent of the city population.

**The result?** Residents have led the delivery of more than 500 projects, events and workshops since the full program began in 2012. Among these are projects that have reduced waste, conserved water and improved energy efficiency. In all, 20,952 residents have participated in various events such as sustainability workshops, regular “sustainability club” meetings, and special events such as neighborhood clean ups that generate collective action from residents.[2] Many more have made specific contributions to individual neighborhood projects. The program has helped to build support for a city-wide sustainability plan and neighborhood projects can now be aligned with targets in the plan.

Now, instead of City Planner, Wachtel is called the City’s Sustainability Manager and he oversees a team of two full time planners, a part-time manager of the Sustainable Neighborhoods Program and two interns who work 1-1-5 hours per week.

Wachtel explains that the program also strengthens positive interactions between residents and the city administration. When people learn projects are part of the program and resident-driven their suspicion about the city’s involvement dissipates, while elected officials and city staff recognize residents from Sustainable Neighborhoods as valuable contributors to city goals.

Nearby cities have adopted the program and Lakewood officials have established an umbrella initiative (and are hoping to create an entity) - the [Sustainable Neighborhood Network](https://www.sustainableneighborhoodnetwork.org/) - to support uptake and share ideas across participating neighborhoods.

**How does it work?**

Neighborhoods are invited to submit applications to join the program. Plans are assessed against criteria that consider the suitability of proposed projects for the neighborhood, how wider resident participation will be encouraged, and how projects address equity and diversity. As Wachtel points out, “the biggest challenge is diversity. We depend on people to volunteer and we don’t see as much equity as we would like in terms of who is leading the programs.”

When an application is approved, the program coordinator makes contact to help get projects off the ground. Through a dedicated program website neighborhoods can track their projects and share news. Approved and completed projects earn credits awarded by the city. When a neighborhood reaches 60 credits they are certified as a Sustainable Neighborhood. To maintain that status beyond one year neighborhoods must continue to participate in the program.

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/62e545c8-7d37-4ab5-a82c-826b84d8e8eb.png)

*Figure 1: Screenshot from the Sustainable Neighborhood Network website depicting project status and summaries (Source:* [*https://www.sustainableneighborhoodnetwork.org/sustainable-neighborhoods-lakewood/belmar/belmar-archived-forms*](https://www.sustainableneighborhoodnetwork.org/sustainable-neighborhoods-lakewood/belmar/belmar-archived-forms)*)*

Participating neighborhoods are recognized through celebratory receptions with the Mayor, the city’s newsletter and speaking opportunities for neighborhood leaders at schools, colleges, and professional conferences. The program’s contributions to the city’s sustainability goals are recorded in an annual report.  The city also offers support for neighborhoods to “relaunch” the program when neighborhoods want to refocus their efforts and renew their leadership.

**Why It Works**

The success of the Sustainable Neighborhoods Program can be attributed to:

1. **A combination of self-selection and selection of participants**: the process for selecting neighborhoods first encourages any willing community to come forward and second, enables the city to allocate limited resources to projects most likely to make a significant contribution to the city’s sustainability goals.
2. **Community empowerment**: By making projects resident-led the program incentivizes participation by offering people a genuine opportunity to shape their local community.
3. **Public recognition**: Certifying neighborhoods and publicizing the achievements of residents generates civic pride that rewards participation in the program.
4. **Training and support**: Technical support, training for neighborhood leaders, and onboarding processes that broaden leadership structures leads to effective projects and sustainable neighborhood participation.
5. **Political support:** The current Lakewood Mayor, Adam Paul, hosted the program pilot in the community he represented as a Council Member and has since backed efforts to expand it.

**Read more about the impact and current status of the Sustainable Neighbhorhoods Program [here](https://mailchi.mp/f66fa43e8a61/neighborhood-credit-update-other-announcements?e=3da4e4d71c)** \[Updated March 4, 2021\].

## End notes

1. Alyssa Vogan, email exchange with the author. “Lakewood, Colorado, Finalist,” Engaged Cities Award, Cities of Service, accessed February 16, 2020, [https://engagedcitiesaward.citiesofservice.org/lakewood-colorado-2019-finalist/](https://engagedcitiesaward.citiesofservice.org/lakewood-colorado-2019-finalist/).
2. This statistic refers to each instance of participation. Some residents participate more than once.
