id: "collective-intelligence:case/listening-to-africa"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "Listening to Africa"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/listening-to-africa"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "To track unfolding crises the World Bank Group used mobile phone surveys to communicate directly with the people experiencing them"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# Listening to Africa

**To track unfolding crises the World Bank Group used mobile phone surveys to communicate directly with the people experiencing them**

- Category: Task Performed
- Topic: Welfare monitoring
- Location: Sub-saharan Africa (Madagascar, Malawi, Senegal, Tanzania, Togo, and Mali)
- Implementation level: national
- Owner: World Bank Group
- Years in operation: 2012-2017
- Platforms: Mobile phone; In-person
- Project website: https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/listening-to-africa
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

Crises, such as disease and famine, spread rapidly if left unreported. Traditional data collection methods, such as in-person surveys, delay responses on the ground. Today, the advent and dissemination of mobile phones, accelerates the process of talking to people who are normally difficult to reach.

The World Bank Group, in collaboration with national statistical offices and NGOs, piloted the use of mobile phone-based surveys for crisis-monitoring in six Sub-Saharan countries. Known collectively as [Listening to Africa](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/listening-to-africa#1) (L2A), the pilots sought to offer development agencies and policymakers more timely data about vulnerable populations. **As mobile phone ownership rates have risen in Africa, mobile telephony has become an important new way to gather data for research and policy.** The World Bank Group stated:

The ultimate aim of the program is to develop a high-frequency phone survey system which could be integrated into national statistical systems, just like censuses, surveys and other administrative data. These surveys strive to complement traditional household surveys and fill in data gaps with more frequent, real-time, high quality representative data on wellbeing in a cost-effective manner.[1]

Between 2012 and 2017, the L2A initiative operated in Madagascar, Malawi, Senegal, Tanzania, Mali and Togo.

**The result?**  **L2A has proven to be a successful example of how collective intelligence can be generated at scale and across a large geography by taking advantage of the common technology of mobile phones and applying it to population surveys.**

For example, in Mali, L2A used mobile phone surveys to monitor the wellbeing of those fleeing civil conflict in the north of the country. The 500 people surveyed included those in refugee camps in neighboring countries, displaced people living in the capital Bamako, and refugees who returned to regional cities as the conflict subsided. Following a baseline survey in July 2014, the mobile phone surveys gathered data on nutrition, employment, social cohesion, and the challenges associated with returning home.[2] The data was shared with decision-makers and used to inform responses such as the design of refugee return programs. In Malawi, L2A established a sample of 1,500 households, covering all but one of the country’s 28 districts. When Malawi was affected by floods in January 2015, mobile phone surveys enabled information about the severity and impact of a major flood to be collected “within a couple of days.”[3]

L2A also found mobile phone surveys could help to tap this type of collective intelligence more frequently and detect problems sooner than methods typically used by statistical agencies. For example, L2A researchers and their in-country partners used mobile phone surveys to:

- track household living conditions for people in Madagascar over 34 rounds of surveying between 2014-2017, including how increasing food insecurity was affecting vulnerable citizens[4]
- collect data as often as twice a month on issues as diverse as education, health and tax in Tanzania in a partnership with a local civil society organization that began in January 2014[5]
- collect monthly data over 24 months on poverty in Senegal to follow up a face-to-face baseline survey in January 2015[6]
- measure change in perceptions about the frequency of power cuts in Togo’s capital, Lome, by comparing the results of a March 2014 baseline survey with a mobile phone survey six months later.[7]

National statistical agencies or the NGO partners also shared L2A data publicly, creating a new resource for decision makers built on information collected directly from those affected by crises.

![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/f02ff5da-a993-4ba3-9329-b34fa2abc21e.png)

*Figure 1: Data from Listening to Madagascar (the country’s Listening to Africa pilot).[8] Data collected through the trials was shared by World Bank Group researchers and through national statistical agencies* (Source: [https://doi.org/10.1596/978-1-4648-0904-0](https://doi.org/10.1596/978-1-4648-0904-0) */* [CC BY 3.0 IGO](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/igo/legalcode)*)*

L2A also found mobile phone surveying could be cost effective, especially for follow up surveys where the initial costs, such as a baseline survey, equipment and setting up a call center, had been accounted for.[9]

Even as the World Bank was rolling out the L2A initiative it was applying what it was learning to other contexts. In [Liberia and Sierra Leone](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-25120-8_2) it used mobile phone surveys to rapidly monitor the socio-economic impacts of the 2014 Ebola crisis.[10] In 2017, it used the same approach to assess the population at risk of famine in the drought and conflict-driven humanitarian crisis concentrated in [Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan, and Yemen](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-25120-8_3).[11]

In 2016, the World Bank Group [published a free guide](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/24595), based on findings from L2A and similar work conducted in other countries, to support the effective implementation of mobile phone surveying in developing countries.

**How did it work?**

The World Bank initially partnered with Twaweza, a Tanzanian NGO in 2010 and 2011. The project aimed to assess what citizens thought about a new constitution for the country using a combination of face-to-face and mobile-phone surveys. This project helped to demonstrate that reliable data could be collected by mobile phone. Between 2012 and 2017 the project was expanded into the full L2A initiative to consolidate, build on and share best practice for mobile phone surveying.

The L2A methodology has four steps:[12]

Step 1: Baseline survey — this is a face-to-face household survey which serves as a baseline, where respondents are identified and core household and respondent characteristics are collected. At this point, the field team distributes a mobile phone (where necessary) to the household and sometimes a solar charger, and the participant is trained to respond to mobile interviews. The households are selected randomly from the country’s population center data, and in many instances did not previously have a phone.

Step 2: Mobile phone survey — following the baseline survey, mobile phone interviews are conducted monthly, starting with respondent verification questions (e.g. name, age, gender). Phone surveys allow for interaction and clarification of questions as need be in case of unclarity on questions and also account for the fact that some household respondents are illiterate. In L2A, phone interviews were conducted by either the World Bank team, or in the case of Madagascar, the NGO Human Network International helped collect responses.

Participants who complete each phone interview are ‘remunerated’ with phone credit (equivalent to about $US1 per interview) transferred directly to their mobile phone after every interview (this is necessary if they do not have phone plans to keep the numbers active and also acts as an incentive for them to continue to respond). Then, 1,500 - 2,000 respondents are called every month for 10-20 minutes to discuss general welfare questions that are tailored each month (the interviews are intended to be flexible and adaptive).[13] The questions are used to assess change in welfare based on the baseline data from step one. In L2A, each household was interviewed by the same interviewer every month in order to create a better relationship and extract better data. In addition, interviewers who could not reach their household tried again throughout the month in order to ensure they responded. They also took down numbers of other members of the household, to make sure they could find alternative ways of reaching the respondent.

The Call Centers where surveying takes place are run either independently or through a think tank or at a statistical office, but enumerators are always well trained and closely supervised to assure data quality.

Step 3: Rapid analysis - once the data has been collected, data cleaning and quality checks are carried out and the data is analyzed. The data from each survey is combined with data from the baseline survey or from earlier rounds to produce as many insights as possible.

Step 4: Dissemination — this step focuses on making the data publicly available in an anonymized form through various channels. In Malawi, Madagascar, Senegal, and Togo, the L2A team worked with the local national statistics offices to create web pages displaying data. They also held monthly dissemination events to share findings from that month with key stakeholders. The [guide](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/24595) developed by the World Bank Group also encourages consideration of press conferences, social media and releasing the data as open data, to aid dissemination. In L2A the aim was to release data within four weeks of the collection process being completed.

**Why It Worked**

The success of Listening to Africa was driven by factors that include:

1. **A compelling goal**: Humanitarian crises in African have long been a global concern. L2A offered data that could help governments and relief agencies to intervene sooner and more effectively.
2. **Equipping participants to complete the task**: Where participants in surveys did not already have a mobile phone they were provided with one and, where required, a solar-powered phone charger. As well as enabling participation this helped survey samples to be representative of the broader population affected by a crisis and made survey results valuable for the partnering statistical agencies.
3. **Small but relevant incentives**: By offering phone credit as the reward for completing an interview, participation in the surveys was able to be maintained over time.
4. **Survey design**: Surveys were designed to be shorter than traditional surveys, about 10-20 minutes, taking into account the risk of connectivity losses and the time cost for participants. This also helped to limit data collection to vital information in volumes that could be quickly processed and shared to guide effective crisis response.
5. **Mobile phone coverage**: In recent years the ownership of mobile phones in Africa has grown rapidly - a 2017 [Pew Research Center Survey](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2018/10/09/majorities-in-sub-saharan-africa-own-mobile-phones-but-smartphone-adoption-is-modest/) found that about four out of five residents of sub-saharan Africa owned at least a basic mobile phone. This was critical for surveying otherwise hard to reach populations.

## End notes

title: "New Start Career Network"

date: "2020-10"
summary: "Network of volunteer career coaches helps long-term unemployed in New Jersey to find a new job"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"

# New Start Career Network

**Network of volunteer career coaches helps long-term unemployed in New Jersey to find a new job**

- Category: Problem Solved
- Topic: Workforce Development
- Location: New Jersey, United States
- Implementation level: State Government
- Owner: John J. Heldrich Center for Workforce Development (Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey)
- Years in operation: 2015 - present
- Platforms: Web; phone; in-person
- Project website: https://www.newstartcareernetwork.org/Home
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

Despite the unemployment rate in the United States reaching a 50-year low in 2019, long-term unemployment - where people are unemployed for over six months - remains a major issue.[1] Long term unemployed job seekers are more likely to remain unemployed and to suffer depression and anxiety. Even those who are re-employed after a stretch of long-term unemployment may end up underemployed, or in roles that underutilize their skills or education, and are often paid less than they were earning previously. Needing to work -- and not being able to find a full-time job -- some end up in multiple part-time jobs to make ends meet.

Since the global financial crisis, older, more experienced, and often well-educated people are joining the ranks of the long-term unemployed. People in this older cohort (age 45+)  face unique barriers to finding a job. In addition to the financial and emotional challenges that can accompany long-term unemployment, older workers often have outdated job search skills and encounter age discrimination when applying for new jobs.[2] Moreover, there are fewer services catering for this demographic, with the limited programs there are typically focused on helping people win entry level jobs or designed for other categories of unemployed job seekers such as the justice-involved, veterans or those with disabilities, who may face daunting but different challenges.

In New Jersey, which has had one of the highest rates of long-term unemployment in the US and where about half of the state’s long-term unemployed are over age 45, researchers have begun exploring ways to support this group of older job seekers.[3] Since 2015, the Heidrich Center for Workforce Development at Rutgers University, one of the nation’s leading action research organizations focused on workforce, has developed a live and web-based coaching program - the [New Start Career Network](https://www.newstartcareernetwork.org/Home) (NSCN) - to provide free assistance to long-term unemployed and underemployed job seekers aged 45 and older.

At the [core of New Start’s offering are volunteer career coaches](https://workingnation.com/do-something-awesome-when-finding-your-job-is-the-job/) who, over a 3-month period, help job seeker “members” of the network to develop career plans and find job opportunities. Coaches also connect job seekers to services that help people to manage their finances and mental health, learn about education and training opportunities, or access resources of partner organizations. Coaching is delivered primarily by phone and free, web-based video conferencing tools (such as Zoom) and complemented by in-person sessions. By using a web-based platform the NSCN is able to assemble the widely distributed expertise of volunteer coaches and match it to the specific needs of older job seekers. The NSCN also gives members access to a collection of online career planning resources.  Maria Heidkamp, Director, New Start Career Network, explains this was a vast improvement on what was previously available:

There were some bootcamp model programs that put long-term unemployed jobseekers through a 5-6 week bootcamp. These were very intensive and had a high cost per job seeker but they could only serve 20-25 people at a time. When we started, New Jersey had about 125,000 people in this category - long-term unemployed...and given our resources, **we needed to figure out how we could use technology to build some way to provide services, at scale, but also provide handholding for people who need that. In other words a combination of ‘high tech and high touch’.**[4]

 **![New Start](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/72d7f552-78e1-4a67-b397-2138efaafbb5.jpg)**

*Figure 1: A New Start Career Network Job Fair where volunteer career coaches are helping job seekers in “Practice your pitch” sessions (Credit: John J. Heldrich Center for Workforce Development).*

**The result?** As of January 2020, the NSCN has 5,100 registered members and 330 volunteer career coaches, with 689 members receiving individual coaching over the first four years of the program. In a 2018 survey of members, two-thirds indicated that the NSCN had improved their motivation, half said it had improved their confidence and emotional well-being, and 86 percent said they would refer the program to a friend.[5] In the words of one job seeker, “It was good to have someone to check in with, to help me come up with goals and actionable items, and to keep me accountable. It’s also good to know you’re not alone.” Another noted, “My coach listened and offered guidance and advice and was always there for me if I needed support, or even just to bounce ideas and thoughts around with.”

The educational profile of NSCN members also supports the contention that a cohort-specific response for older, more educated job seekers is needed, with 44 percent of members holding a bachelor’s degree and 33 percent holding a Master’s degree or higher. The program is open to all job seekers, however, including those with high school degrees or less.  The Heidrich Center is currently conducting an analysis to assess the NSCN’s effect on employment outcomes with results expected to be available later in 2020.

Volunteer coaches recruited to the program bring diverse professional backgrounds, valuable personal experiences, and are geographically dispersed. This enables NSCN to better match a coach’s capabilities with an individual job seeker’s needs and ambitions. For example, some coaches are HR professionals, others are industry experts from IT, finance, healthcare, pharma, education and other sectors. In one case, NSCN matched a volunteer coach with a background in international marketing with a job seeker who was trying to get back into import/export and logistics and distribution work. In another case, a volunteer coach who holds an MBA in finance has worked with several job seekers seeking related positions. Some job seekers are seeking a coach who will be task-oriented and help keep them accountable; others are hoping for help exploring alternative career possibilities.  In addition to their professional backgrounds, many of the volunteers have either dealt with job loss themselves or have experience in interacting with people who are long-term unemployed. With coaches located across North, Central and South Jersey, and a handful from New York and Philadelphia, matches between coaches and job seekers from the same or nearby communities can also be achieved. Job seekers are given a choice of virtual or in-person coaching, with the caveat that virtual coaching makes it much easier to make a match.

In 2018, in recognition of their extraordinary volunteer efforts to help New Jersey’s long-term unemployed job seekers, the NSCN Volunteer Career Coaches were honored with a NJ State Governor’s Jefferson Award. The Jefferson Awards were established in 1972 as the official recognition program of the United States Senate and are considered America’s highest honor for public service and volunteerism. In NSCN’s first four years, the coaches collectively donated over 40,000 hours to helping job seekers.

The NSCN has also attracted a wide range of collaborators from the government, business and community sectors who support and advocate for older job seekers. A major partner is Rutgers University Career Services, which has provided access to several online tools such as Vault and Sokanu and assists with employer recruitment for NSCN’s fall and spring members-only job fairs. There are various employer, industry or business association partners that often help promote or participate in NSCN’s job fairs or post jobs on the website or in the Tip of the Week email blast. Government partners in New Jersey include the Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Governor’s Office of Volunteerism, which provides financial support to NSCN through a federal Volunteer Generation Fund grant, Community College Consortium and both the State Library and the NJ Library Association. Community partners include the Mental Health Association of New Jersey, job clubs, older adult service and advocacy organizations, and veterans employment programs.

Key staff at the Heidrich Center involved with NSCN have also helped to shape government workforce development policy through their participation on the [advisory council for New Jersey’s jobs strategy](http://www.heldrich.rutgers.edu/newsroom/governor-murphy-announces-plan-expand-opportunities-new-jersey-career-seekers-and-employers). Launched in January 2020, [Jobs NJ](https://www.njeda.com/about/Public-Information/Economic-Plan-(1))  recognizes the unemployed, underemployed and those out of the labor market as “underutilized talent pools” that offer opportunities to strengthen the state’s competitive advantage in talent.[6]

**How does it work?**

Job seekers have learned about NSCN through several sources including newspaper and radio coverage when the program was launched, word-of-mouth, through presentations at job clubs and libraries, and referrals from partners and other programs including from One Stop Career Centers. All job seekers sign up on the website; in a few cases, public libraries have assisted job seekers who have limited computer skills.

At the [sign up page](https://www.newstartcareernetwork.org/Sign-In?action=register) job seekers are asked to verify their eligibility to become a member of the NSCN by confirming their state of residence (must be a resident of New Jersey) and birth year (must be 45 years of age or over). Once eligibility is confirmed a short series of questions gathers information about the job seeker’s unemployment benefit status, highest level of education, recent work history, and internet access, all of which is used to personalize the support members receive.

Upon logging in, job seeker members can access [online support](https://www.newstartcareernetwork.org/Job-Seekers) such as:

- Online resources covering how to conduct a “modern” job search, update a resume and perform well in job interviews, and which provide information about job opportunities and local support services such as job clubs and training.
- Webinars with content developed specifically for midcareer and older job seekers over 45 years of age who are long-term unemployed
- Opportunities to connect with peers via Facebook and LinkedIn
- Invitations to in-person career events and job fairs and weekly job search tips.

Job seekers who opt to work with a volunteer career coach are matched with a coach based on several factors including whether they are open to virtual instead of in-person coaching, industry background (where possible), and whether they need help with specific tasks (such as improving their LinkedIn profile) or more general assistance with accountability and motivation.  Volunteer coaches are asked to commit to 2-4 hours a week for 6 months, although many of the volunteers have continued with NSCN for one or more years. Before starting as a coach, they must complete a 6-hour in-person orientation and training session, which includes information about the labor market, the professional and personal challenges older and long-term unemployed job seekers face, such as age discrimination and lack of self esteem and confidence, and an overview of contemporary job search and basic coaching techniques. Coaches are recruited through the Rutgers University Alumni Associations, human resources professional associations, community partners, and through a [standing call](https://www.newstartcareernetwork.org/volunteers/become-a-volunteer) on the NSCN website.[7] The NSCN also has an online Coaching Community of Practice that helps to build the capability of all coaches.

NSCN coaches have experimented with a variety of small group virtual coaching sessions focused on resilience, keeping positive during a job search, pursuing entrepreneurship, coping with transitions, and mens’ and womens’ groups.

Major funding for the NSCN is supplied by the Philip and Tammy Murphy Family Foundation, with additional support from a range of business and community organizations including New Jersey Resources, the Fund for New Jersey, and the Corporation for National and Community Service/New Jersey Volunteer Generation Fund.

**Why It Works**

1. **Tapping people’s intelligence and expertise:** By taking advantage of the skills, experience and expertise of other professionals, New Start is able to provide better services by matching coaches to long-term unemployed members with comparable backgrounds and goals.
2. **Supporting powerful intrinsic incentives:** Maria Heidkamp explains that the primary motivation for the coaches to participate is “knowing that the work they’re doing is extremely meaningful” and that NSCN responds to this by “empower\[ing\] coaches to use their creativity, problem solving skills and empathy in ways that some other volunteer assignments don’t always do.”
3. **Volunteer training and support**: Coaches are equipped to provide support that job seekers value through mandatory initial training and then ongoing support through peer networks focused on improving coaching practice.
4. **Widely accessible and targeted online resources**: To increase the number of older job seekers who can access support, resources are made available online and developed specifically for older, long-term unemployed job seekers.

## End notes

Cohen, P., [“Lots of Job Hunting, but No Job, Despite Low Unemployment”](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/31/business/economy/long-term-unemployed.html), The New York Times, 31 Oct 2019

id: "collective-intelligence:case/the-bristol-approach"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "The Bristol Approach"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/the-bristol-approach"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "Bristol citizens work with nonprofit arts organisation to collect and analyse air quality data"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"

# The Bristol Approach

**Bristol citizens work with nonprofit arts organisation to collect and analyse air quality data**

- Category: Problem Solved
- Topic: Air pollution
- Location: Bristol, United Kingdom
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: Knowle West Media Centre; Ideas for Change; Bristol City Council
- Years in operation: 2015-present
- Platforms: In-person; mobile app
- Project website: https://www.bristolapproach.org/bristol-approach-projects/air-quality/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

“Bristol remains a city of challenges,” said Mayor Marvin Rees at Bristol’s [annual State of the City Address](https://www.bristol247.com/news-and-features/news/bristol-remains-city-challenges/) in 2017. But Bristol is responding to its challenges by supporting communities to work with technologists and data ‘experts’ to gather information about on-the-ground conditions, especially air quality.

**In 2015 the city created** [**The Bristol Approach**](https://www.bristolapproach.org/bristol-approach-projects/air-quality/)**, a “citizen sensing” method for running community-driven projects that use sensor technologies and local knowledge to understand and develop solutions to urban issues.** The Approach’s six-step framework allows citizens to work as “sensors” to gather information to address key problems collaboratively, build community and foster relationships between residents and public servants.

**Background**

In 2015 [Knowle West Media Centre](http://kwmc.org.uk/) (KWMC), a nonprofit arts organization that supports people to use technology and the arts to develop creative solutions to challenges, began working with communities in East Bristol to explore how technology could be used to help tackle the issues they were concerned about.

KWMC’s initial pilot was part of the REPLICATE Project, a five-year European funded project exploring how ‘smart’ technology could benefit people and neighbourhoods. The REPLICATE Project in Bristol is led by Bristol City Council. The pilot followed The Bristol Approach - a six-step framework devised by KWMC and the Barcelona-based innovation company Ideas for Change, with support from the Bristol City Council.

In the pilot, KWMC worked with artists to hold a series of informal, creative face-to-face conversations with residents in South Bristol and East Bristol at popular “hotspots” such as community spaces, nail salons, and cafes to identify issues people cared about, eventually settling on damp homes as the issue that generated the greatest interest from participants.[1]

KWMC then supported residents to develop a data collection system, where volunteers used sensors -- hardware co-created at KWMC workshops with artists and others from the community -- to measure dampness in their homes by recording temperature and humidity data. The findings were then presented to the City Council, along with proposed measures on how landlords and tenants could work together to improve the situation. The entire pilot process took approximately a year and a half.[2]

Learning from this first pilot informed a second pilot in East Bristol as part of the REPLICATE Project, beginning in 2016 and focusing on the Ashley, Easton and Lawrence Hill wards.[3] Certain areas experienced heavy traffic flow and residents had voiced concerns about air quality and a lack of awareness of the impact that air pollution was having on their health.

![Bristol 1](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/df57c349-a99c-4492-86e8-ec124bc60c52.jpg)

*Figure 1: The “ladybird” air quality sensor (Source:* [https://www.bristolapproach.org/bristol-approach-projects/air-quality/](https://www.bristolapproach.org/bristol-approach-projects/air-quality/))

**The result?**

From 2016 to date (February 2020) KWMC engaged over 850 people with the process of ’citizen sensing’. In both the damp homes and air quality pilot projects, co-creation design sessions produced novel sensor designs embraced by participants. Six families tested the “ladybird” air quality sensor and accompanying mobile app. The portable “ladybird” air quality sensor could be attached to bicycles, bags, and car windscreens in order to gather nitrogen dioxide data. Academics from the University of the West of England (UWE) Computer Science department worked to develop hardware and software that people could use on their phones to connect to these physical mobile sensors. Thirteen community buildings in east Bristol were also fitted with air quality sensors, built using inexpensive [Luftdaten](https://luftdaten.info/en/home-en/) sensor kits. As the air quality project was completed only recently, the data produced has yet to prompt any decisive government action, but the city council and KWMC are actively considering its potential uses.

In the meantime, select community members are using the learnings to inspire real change, seeking out “cleaner” travel routes or changing their own travel behavior, with some even giving away their cars. In one particularly illustrative case, Sioban (a pseudonym), learned of the project on social media and wanted to get involved so she began to collect data using the ladybird sensor. In 2019, she attended a ‘Making sense of your data’ workshop with KWMC to learn how to interpret the data she gathered. Initially Sioban wanted to get involved when she noticed that she had developed breathing issues after changing her daily cycling commute from the countryside to the center of Bristol. When the doctors told her that the level of pollution in her lungs from inhaling poor quality air in the neighborhood she cycled through was equivalent to smoking two cigarettes daily, she changed her route and saw her breathing improve.

Realizing that topography and minor route changes can seriously influence air quality and its effect on your health, Sioban wanted to gather data to improve the quality of urban life around Bristol. “As an architect, I can use that information when I am designing spaces and actively respond to how people are experiencing and perceiving public spaces,” said Sioban, “and hopefully that would improve the public spaces.”[4]

The Bristol Approach has also been used by young adults  to collect data surrounding other issues, including mental health and food waste.

**How does it work?**

KWMC is the Bristol Living Lab and a member of the [European Network of Living Labs](https://enoll.org/). As the Bristol Living Lab, KWMC provides support and a space where people from different backgrounds can come together to innovate, experiment and address social challenges.

KWMC uses an ‘action research’ process – a specific approach to research that does not start with a fixed ‘hypothesis’ to test but with an idea that could be explored further. The Bristol Approach framework is inspired by KWMC’s practice: rather than ‘pushing’ technology or pre-determined ‘solutions’ onto people, KWMC works with local people, artists, technologists and other partners to ‘pull in’ the resources needed to develop ideas and tools for tackling local challenges and creating new opportunities.

The air quality pilot followed the six steps of the Bristol Approach:

**Step 1: Identification (March 2017 - July 2017)** — KWMC held several in-person events in the Ashley, Easton, Lawrence Hill areas of east Bristol where citizens and organizations could discuss community issues. These events included workshops, community meetings, one-on-one conversations, and working in community venues.

**Step 2: Framing (September 2017 - October 2017)** —  Several issues related to air quality emerged as a particular concern for five groups: cyclists, schoolchildren/parents, taxi drivers, social housing tenants, and community venues.[5] The issues included a lack of knowledge of local air quality, concerns about links between air quality and health, and fumes created by idling cars.  KWMC acknowledged how the lack of information and data about air quality in Bristol prevented the community from developing measures to mitigate the debilitating health effects.

**Step 3: Design (November 2017 - January 2018)** — KWMC then led issue-based design and making sessions with each of the groups to “identify the problem they wanted to explore in more detail, the data they wanted to collect, and how to go about it.” The groups developed ideas for how to design and implement air quality sensors to collect data on-the-go, and worked with an artist to design prototypes (shaped like a ladybird) which were created at KWMC’s digital manufacturing space, KWMC: The Factory. The groups also deliberated on how the data would be stored and shared. They worked with KWMC and [Data Unity](https://www.watershed.co.uk/studio/projects/data-unity) to establish a privacy and data sharing agreement that was then used on the mobile app that was linked to the ladybird sensors.

**Step 4: Deployment (March 2018 - February 2019)** — Six of the portable ladybird citizens were deployed and tested by citizens, who were encouraged to act as “human sensors,” recording their movements and experiences to provide context for the statistical data.[6] Thirteen stationary Luftdaten sensors were also placed in community buildings and spaces. During this period, KWMC also held events such as “Women, Bikes & Bristol” to engage groups that aren’t typically heard when it comes to “smart technology” initiatives.

**Step 5: Orchestration (March 2019 onwards)** — In March 2019, KWMC ran three workshops to teach 21 Bristol residents to analyze the data they were collecting from the sensors.[7] Once it was time to visualize the data, KWMC digital fabrication experts worked with participants to design ways to tell their data stories to the community in-person and online. For example, one group made a “travel air gauge” based on a see-saw in order to encourage residents to base their transport choices on balancing the scale of their choices’ environmental impact.

**Step 6: Outcome (March 2019 onwards)** — KWMC and the participants worked with digital artists and technologists to design visualizations of the air quality data that was gathered at one of the community spaces—a primary school in Easton. The artist used different colors to represent levels of nitrogen dioxide, ozone, and particulate matter observed every 15 minutes over 28 days. These visualizations were placed on postcards and distributed around east Bristol, and other participating spaces could view the data on an online open source platform developed by Data Unity. As an arts organization, KWMC emphasizes the importance of presenting information in a way that is visually appealing and easier to understand than complicated charts.[8]

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/5d47bd70-51ea-46dd-ad41-aed15d2e48f7.png)*

*Figure 2: The Six-Step Framework of the Bristol Approach (Source:* [*https://kwmc.org.uk/projects/bristolapproach/*](https://kwmc.org.uk/projects/bristolapproach/)*)*

Employing artists to work on the project is a key aspect that sets the Bristol Approach apart from traditional research projects and studies. According to Carolyn Hassan, founder and director of Knowle West Media Centre, the artists were able to create more fun, expressive, and engaging ways to work with people throughout the project. This helped them dig deeper to the root of the city’s issues and citizen’s concerns, and design and engagement in which citizens felt more inclined to contribute. KWMC views citizen sensing as “a process where citizens build, use, or act as sensors to gather information that will help them to tackle an issue that’s important to them.”[9] Thus, the goal of this project was to help people in Bristol use digital tools to learn more about their environment and explore new ways of sensing their surroundings.

This process of designing sensors and gathering and analyzing air quality data concludes phase one of the air quality pilot. Though the precise details of what phase two entails have yet to be finalized and publicized, it is likely going to explore questions such as: how can citizens combine air quality data with data on other types of pollution such as noise or other quality data such as water, how they can implement multiple types of sensors such as primitive or complex designs, and how they can be tech-agnostic to adapt to different situations and continue to work efficiently with citizens.

**Why It Works**

> *“If there is one thing I would underline about the Bristol Approach, it’s that it is a work in progress. We are still learning and still gathering data as we engage with communities and build trust, all to the end of improving the approach’s effectiveness. In order to learn more and grow, you need to build trust and deepen the engagement with communities” — Carolyn Hassan, founder and director, Knowle West Media Centre*

1. **Collaboration:** Citizens, developers, community organizations, researchers, technologists, and more, are involved in the design and testing of products and processes. Experts worked with citizens directly in events, workshops, and more, to train them in data collection and guide their outputs while ensuring they feel valued and their local expertise is recognised.
2. **Equal emphasis on data and people:** When collected, stored, and analyzed properly, data can be a valuable resource for administrations and general problem-solvers to leverage for informing and solving crucial issues - and also for communities wanting to understand a particular problem. However, data is not useful if it does not ultimately serve people. Hence the minds behind the Bristol Approach took care to ensure the data being collected was addressing the issues people truly cared about, and that human behavior was considered just as heavily as technology.
3. **Collective action and use of latent resources:** Now, Bristol’s local administration has key data on air pollution. This data combined with other community resources such as expertise, technology, and relationships can all be used for future efforts. The social issues explored in the problem identification phase that do not advance to the next stage are placed in an open access repository to be used by other interested parties in the future.[10] Equipped with this new information, government, businesses, and residents can all work together to drive change toward cleaner air and solve related public problems.

## End notes

2. Balestrini, Mara, Yvonne Rogers, Carolyn Hassan, Javi Creus, Martha King, and Paul Marshall, “A City in Common: A Framework to Orchestrate Large-Scale Citizen Engagement around Urban Issues,” In Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems  - CHI ’17, 2282–94. Denver, Colorado, USA: ACM Press, 2017..[https://uclic.ucl.ac.uk/content/6-news-events-seminars/20170502-ucl-will-have-a-great-presence-at-chi-2017/balestrini.paper.pdf](https://uclic.ucl.ac.uk/content/6-news-events-seminars/20170502-ucl-will-have-a-great-presence-at-chi-2017/balestrini.paper.pdf).
3. The EU awarded this funding to Bristol as part of the city’’s contribution to the [REPLICATE Project](https://replicate-project.eu/) --a five-year initiative to develop innovative approaches to sustainability. The cities of Bristol, Florence and San Sebastian led the project.

# Governador Pergunta (Governor Asks)

**Governor Asks uses online and face-to-face outreach to engage almost a quarter million participants in one month**

- Category: CI How-to
- Topic: Public Health Care, Traffic Safety
- Location: Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
- Implementation level: State Government
- Owner: State Government of Rio Grande do Sul
- Years in operation: 2011 - 2012
- Platforms: All Our Ideas (web and mobile); In-person
- Project website: http://web.archive.org/web/20131129155101/http:/gabinetedigital.rs.gov.br/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

On November 30, 2012 Tarso Genro, Governor of the Brazillian state of Rio Grande do Sul, a southern state with eleven million residents, met with dozens of state authorities, members of the media, and ordinary citizens to discuss solutions to the state’s traffic safety problem. This historic in-person meeting was the culmination of the [largest digital consultation](http://web.archive.org/web/20121204144716/http:/gabinetedigital.rs.gov.br/post/5248/) in Brazil’s history, known as Governador Pergunta (“Governor Asks”). Over a one-month period citizens were tasked with proposing ideas to reduce by half the 2,300 traffic fatalities that occurred annually in the state by 2020.[1] **Using the online All Our Ideas platform, a so-called wiki survey platform on which people choose repeatedly between two answer choices to arrive at a rank-ordered list of responses, 100,000 people cast 240,000 online votes on 2,000 proposals over the course of a month to inform the creation of major state policies.** To garner widespread participation, this online consultation took an innovative approach to outreach that blended online and offline elements, including citizen engagement mobile vans, making it more diverse and inclusive while still achieving scale.

**Background**

Rio Grande do Sul has a rich history of innovative citizen engagement initiatives. The state’s capital, Porto Alegre, hosted the world’s first participatory budgeting initiative in 1989. A similar participatory budgeting program was run at the state level between 1999 and 2002. Governor Genro created the 'Gabinete Digital’ (Digital Cabinet) in 2011 to institutionalize an online version of the participatory budgeting program while also launching three new initiatives:

- Governor Asks – a space for citizens to make policy proposals in response to a challenge identified by the state, and to vote on which proposals should be prioritized by the state government
- Governor Responds - a platform in which the governor responded to the inquiries raised in the Governor Asks sessions. Each month, the governor responded to the question that received the most votes in a video.
- Governor Listens - a series of public audiences (broadcast live online) in which the governor and citizens came together to discuss issues of importance to the public.

The road fatalities consultation was the culmination of a series of such online engagements using All Our Ideas. The first iteration of Governor Asks ran in 2011 and collected suggestions for how to improve public health care. The topic was chosen because healthcare had previously been identified as a priority in the state’s participatory budgeting vote for that year.[2] The first iteration of Governor Asks collected over 1,300 proposals and 122,000 votes on public health care within a period of 30 days. The authors of the 50 proposals that received the most votes were invited to meet with Governor Genro at Piratini Palace to further discuss and debate the proposals.[3]

The second iteration of Governor Asks ran in 2012 and focused on traffic safety. In [alignment](https://www.un.org/Docs/journal/asp/ws.asp?m=A/RES/64/255) with the United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety Global Action Plan, the state aimed to reduce by half the number of traffic fatalities by 2020.

**The result?**

During the road fatality engagement, not only did participation double in size, resulting in over 2,000 policy proposals and more than 240,000 votes, but the Genro government then selected ten priority projects to consider implementing.

*![Governador 1](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/c9bc41cc-8d94-4f97-8f11-3f57e0aaf6ce.png)*

*Figure 1: The 2012 meeting between Governor Genro and participants at Piratini Palace (Source:* [*https://blog.allourideas.org/post/75399372139/the-governor-asks-again*](https://blog.allourideas.org/post/75399372139/the-governor-asks-again)*)*

The state government responded to each of the ten priority proposals. Governor Genro met with the authors of the 50 contributions that received the most votes. The public meeting took place at Piratini Palace, the seat of power for the state’s executive, and provided a further platform to publicize the project. Then the Governor referred a proposal to the relevant state committee or agency to take action on the proposal. One citizen who participated in the program, Ricardo Ferriera, asked for 24-hour healthcare clinics. In response, the government opened an emergency clinic in the Lindoia neighborhood. The state also created free bus and metro passes for low income students.

**How did it work?**

The first iteration of Governor Asks ran from November 9 to December 9, 2011. During the first phase of the process, users submitted policy proposals to improve public health care through the Digital Cabinet’s website ([http://www.gabinetedigital.rs.gov.br/](http://www.gabinetedigital.rs.gov.br/)). The website was open for submissions between November 9th and November 28th. Citizens were asked to submit proposals according to five themes: Family Health, Comprehensive Care, Urgency and Emergency, Access to Medicines and Health in Your Region. The second iteration ran for a similar time frame in 2012, with traffic safety proposals grouped into five categories: Education, Road Safety, Communication, Legislation, and Health. These categories were chosen to align with the five thematic chambers of the State Mobilization Committee for Road Safety, the body charged with implementing the state’s road safety action plan.[4]

During the second phase of Governor Asks, which lasted from November 28 to December 10, users voted on policy proposals using the wiki voting platform [All Our Ideas](https://www.allourideas.org/) to decide which 10 policy proposals were of greatest priority for the state government. This open source platform uses a pairwise voting approach, meaning that users are repeatedly presented with two randomized options and asked to choose the one they prefer. Users can also choose that they do not prefer either option, or opt to add a new idea. Thus, participants are voting as between a series of proposals pre-populated by the state or added by participants. As these new ideas are incorporated into the survey, the survey becomes more adaptive to users’ preferences as voting goes on. For example, when the New York City Mayor’s office used All Our Ideas to collect feedback on a sustainability plan, eight of the top ten ideas were voter contributions.

![Governador 2](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/c370e204-c5fd-428c-9e14-887bd6492c15.png)

*Figure 2: The All Our Ideas interface with a pair of proposals (Source:* [*https://blog.allourideas.org/post/14248022671/governor-genro-tops-president-obama-on-citizen*](https://blog.allourideas.org/post/14248022671/governor-genro-tops-president-obama-on-citizen)*)*

The simplicity of the interface and the ease of clicking between two options helped to attract such large numbers of participants. In addition to the wiki survey mechanism, participants were also reached through in-person outreach. Most notably, the Digital Cabinet operated a “voting van” equipped with tablets, laptop computers, and Internet access to collect survey responses from across the state. This broadened the opportunity to participate to those without access to the Internet at home. The Digital Cabinet reports that 20,000 people participated in face-to-face activities (such as meetings with public health care leaders) during the first iteration of Governor Asks, while 10,000 people accessed the voting website from the voting van.[5] The second Governor Asks initiative employed two voting vans, which traveled 1,500 kilometers and visited 22 cities. There were also 150 fixed locations across the state, for instance at Driver Trainer Centers or government agency offices, where participants could go to vote online.[6] The 2012 initiative also employed a modified version of All Our Ideas that worked better on tablets.[7]

[![Governador 3](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/7476f7e3-f0d6-46d8-a242-5a26b9dad799.png)]

*Figure 3: Participants access All Our Ideas inside a voting van (Source:* [*https://blog.allourideas.org/post/75399372139/the-governor-asks-again*](https://blog.allourideas.org/post/75399372139/the-governor-asks-again)*)*

**Why It Worked**

1. **Adaptive Outreach**: Rather than simply writing-off those without reliable access to the Internet, the Digital Cabinet made a concerted effort to engage this population in the Governor Asks initiative through the use of voting vans. As this disconnected population may otherwise have been completely unaware of the initiative had outreach only been done through online or traditional media, in-person outreach was key to garnering over 350,000 votes across the two iterations of the program. The usability improvements made to the tablet version of the platform in the second year also indicate that the Digital Cabinet was receptive to users’ feedback.
2. **Well-Designed Voting System**: Governor Asks made good use of the All Our Ideas platform, most notably its pairwise design. One of the major design benefits is that it requires participants to directly compare two options, instead of allowing them to say they like or dislike several options to the same degree. Unlike a single column survey, in which a small group of voters can push a single proposal to the top of the list, pairwise comparisons ensure that the proposals on the top of the list are a more accurate representation of public sentiment. This design feature helped the Governor to gain a complete and accurate understanding of citizens’ concerns and priorities.
3. **Public Support:** The direct involvement and support of Governor Genro was instrumental to attracting engagement in the initiative. His involvement and promotion reinforced the assertion that people’s participation would matter. Most notably, the opportunity to meet with the Governor in front of the media at Piritani Palace provided a strong incentive for participants to submit relevant and compelling proposals. The Governor’s unwavering commitment to the program, even in the wake of push back against the program from within the government and outside of it, also lent it legitimacy.[8]

type: "GovLab case study"
title: "Smarter Crowdsourcing for Zika"
url: "https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/smarter-crowdsourcing-for-zika"
date: "2020-10"
summary: "To combat the Zika virus the Governance Lab collaborated with national and local government partners to crowdsource solutions from global experts"
source: "The GovLab (collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"

# Smarter Crowdsourcing for Zika

**To combat the Zika virus the Governance Lab collaborated with national and local government partners to crowdsource solutions from global experts**

- Category: CI How-to
- Topic: Public Health
- Location: Virtual
- Implementation level: National, city
- Owner: Inter-American Development Bank, The Governance Lab, Governments of Panama, Colombia, Argentina, Rio de Janeiro
- Years in operation: 2016
- Platforms: Zoom
- Project website: https://zika.smartercrowdsourcing.org/en/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

Problems such as Mosquito-Borne Diseases (MBDs) require innovative actions. To foster transformation in how governments address health and social issues, the Governance Lab based at New York University (The GovLab) in collaboration with government partners and with the support of the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) launched “Smarter Crowdsourcing for Zika” in 2016. Smarter Crowdsourcing is a method for tapping the knowledge of worldwide experts to find implementable and innovative solutions to public problems. Typically, policymakers everywhere are facing a crisis of agility - namely the ability to identify, implement and test innovations in response to new challenges quickly.  **The Zika crisis created the momentum and the motive to do things differently. The five-step Smarter Crowdsourcing method combines the agility and diversity of crowdsourcing (also called open innovation) with curation to target those with relevant know-how and bring them together in a format designed to produce effective and implementable outcomes.**

**Background**

The IADB and The GovLab partnered with the governments of Panama, Colombia, Argentina, and the City of Rio de Janeiro to host a series of online conferences to tap the collective intelligence of local and global experts with relevant skills, experience, and background to come up with innovative and implementable ideas to fight Zika. Instead of organizing a multi-day conference in one physical location which would require participants to arrange for travel and accommodations, and require organizers to secure a venue—all at great expense—these conferences were held online. This reduced overhead, encouraged greater, more diverse and egalitarian participation while reducing climate footprint.

**To avoid thinking too big, The GovLab broke down the challenge of mosquito-borne diseases into sixteen smaller, clearer, better defined and more solvable problems.**

It partnered with the city government of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil and the national governments of Argentina, Colombia, and Panama to find solutions. Partner governments selected six of the 16 to address: Assessing Public Awareness; Communication and Behavior Change; Predictive Analytics; Trash and Standing Water; Information Collection/Data Governance; and Long-term Care.

For instance, The GovLab started from the intractable issue of Zika to articulate the relatively simple question of how to improve the collection of trash in a given city. At the base of the Zika problem – among other things – a failure to pick up garbage led to an accumulation of standing water and mosquito breeding. Once The GovLab was able to articulate more manageable problems, it could then crowdsource help from global experts to devise solutions such as developing adaptive vehicles for improved pickup, using drones to conduct trash surveillance and working with companies to change popular packaging to reduce the incidence of water accumulation.

**The result?**

The [Smarter Crowdsourcing for Zika](https://zika.smartercrowdsourcing.org/en/) project brought together a hundred participants in various fields of expertise from six continents to brainstorm the best ideas to combat the Zika virus. These conferences resulted in a total of 20 recommendations grouped under the six problem areas. The Smarter Crowdsourcing team subsequently conducted further research into these 20 recommendations—including identifying costs and benefits, determining the necessary steps and timetables for implementation, and identifying key strategic decisions—with the assurance that the participating governments would prioritize the recommendations they were most interested in pursuing. With this in mind, the endeavor culminated in an Implementation Report designed to enable public authorities to translate these recommendations into practical, implementable improvements in the way they deliver public health policies and services.[1]

**How Did It Work?**

Between August and October 2016, The GovLab organized six online dialogues over two months in response to each problem - attracting more than 100 global experts, who deliberated online to deepen understanding of the problems and their root causes and to identify solutions. The conferences each lasted two hours and were focused on a particular aspect of the Zika crisis.

These six topics were:

1. Assessing Public Awareness - What are the most effective ways to capture the public’s understanding of mosquito-borne diseases, and how do we use these findings to inform the design of campaigns to improve public awareness?
2. Communication and Behavior Change - What are the most effective ways to change public behavior to prevent mosquito breeding and mosquito bites, and expand access to proper healthcare?
3. Trash and Standing Water - What can be done to eliminate uncollected waste and standing water where mosquitoes breed?
4. Information Collection and Data Governance - How do we develop better practices and policies for epidemiological data collection and for sharing data with the appropriate authorities?
5. Long Term Care - How do we provide support to families with members at risk or already suffering from the chronic effects of Zika and other mosquito-borne diseases?
6. Predictive Analytics - What innovative approaches are available for using data to predict factors influencing outbreaks?

After the conclusion of these conferences, participating governments chose those ideas they were most interested in pursuing.

![Zika 1](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/1655bdee-98f0-4623-8a22-303931f617da.png)

*Figure 1: Topics for the six online conferences which were organized by The GovLab (Source:* [*zika.smartercrowdsourcing.org*](https://zika.smartercrowdsourcing.org/en/)*)*

The Smarter Crowdsourcing team subsequently conducted further interviews and research into these ideas, identifying their costs and benefits, the steps required for implementation, and the key strategic decisions that governments would need to make along the way. The team’s findings were then combined into an Implementation Report comprising twenty initiatives selected for their importance and potential impact as well as their suitability for immediate implementation. This Implementation Report was designed to enable public authorities to translate these new ideas into practical improvements in the way they deliver policies and services.

![Zika 2](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/975b75bf-2658-4a1f-8926-245b6b21af85.png)

*Figure 2: The Smarter Crowdsourcing Zika Report (Source: [zika.smartercrowdsourcing.org](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/zika.smartercrowdsourcing.org))*

The Smarter Crowdsourcing method comprises five, clearly defined steps. These helped to ensure that the expertise solicited was relevant and useful:

1. Partner and Problem Identification: The GovLab, IDB and the Latin American government partners identified and prioritized the core problems to address. Each selected topic was the subject of an online conference.
2. Problem Definition: GovLab briefed each challenge in English, Spanish and Portuguese. Briefings were posted online for public comment. The briefings informed the agenda and discussion for the online dialogues.
3. Curating Guests: Diverse experts and innovators – from practitioners and technologists to policymakers and researchers – were identified and invited to participate in one or more online conferences, matching their expertise to the topics. Guests were asked for recommendations of additional experts who should participate. The focus was on finding those with innovative yet practical approaches to tackling identified problems.
4. Online Conferences: Online conferences -- each one of them focused on a specific problem -- brought together experts with partner government officials to brainstorm innovative and practical ways to tackle the problems. Videos, transcripts and post-conference briefings of each discussion to be posted online for comment.
5. Development of Implementation Plans: The expertise shared during the conferences was integrated into a set of action plans for the government partners. Government partners identified the most viable solutions shared by experts and the GovLab continued working with experts to refine suggestions for implementation.

![Zika 3](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/e545b610-b104-4afd-921b-394ca4feb682.png)

*Figure 3: The Smarter Crowdsourcing methodology (Source: [smartercrowdsourcing.org](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/smartercrowdsourcing.org))*

**Why It Worked**

Smarter Crowdsourcing was successful at attracting useful ideas from leading global experts in a timely fashion because:

1. **Time-bounded participation**: Experts did not have to travel and only needed to participate in the online conference and a follow-up interview.
2. **Government participated together with experts:** Relevant officials from partner countries and cities joined the deliberation to answer questions about on-the-ground conditions and make clear that information provided would be used.
3. **Process for going from idea to implementation**: The initial work on researching and defining concrete problems combined with expert deliberation and further research helped to produce useful and implementable expertise.
4. **Building a network of experts**: The method helps public servants grow a network of knowledgeable and motivated people who are increasingly willing to lend their collective intelligence to difficult issues and reinforces the belief that even a small contribution can make a big difference.
5. **Creating implementation plans**: Significant effort was spent on measuring the costs, benefits, timeframes, political will, and overall ease of implementation for each recommendation to increase the chance that proposal would become policy.

## End notes

1. The full report can be found [here](https://zika.smartercrowdsourcing.org/en/files/smarter-crowdsouring-for-zika-and-other-mosquito-borne-diseases.pdf).
