# vTaiwan

**Reaching consensus using collective intelligence**

- Category: Level of Institutionalization
- Topic: Digital Economy Regulation
- Location: Taiwan
- Implementation level: National
- Owner: g0v, a civic hacker activist group
- Years in operation: 2015 - present
- Platforms: vTaiwan, a purpose-built platform that uses Pol.is among other tools; in-person
- Project website: https://vtaiwan.tw/
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

**Introduction**

vTaiwan is a four-stage online and offline process in which the public and government work collaboratively to create legislation relating to the digital economy. The project is managed by g0v.tw (pronounced “Gov Zero”), the country’s largest civic technology organization, with political support from Taiwan’s Digital Ministry and parliament. Since vTaiwan launched in 2015, more than 200,000 people have participated, resulting in 26 pieces of legislation passed through Taiwan’s parliament. Though not institutionalized by a regulatory framework, the platform has achieved a high degree of staying power by remaining a volunteer-run, transparent process that has grown over time and “survived” a presidential election. While vTaiwan enables citizen engagement throughout the legislative process, it is a good example of collectively defining the problem because the collective intelligence of the vTaiwan community is used to better understand and come to consensus around regulatory issues related to Taiwan’s digital economy, which the community then works to solve with the input of external stakeholders.

**Background**

*How it All Started*

In March 2014, a group of young activists began a three-week occupation of the Taiwanese Parliament in Taipei in response to the Cross-Strait Service Trade Agreement, which would have liberalized trade with China and which, despite strong public protest, the country’s parliament had negotiated behind closed doors. This series of sit-ins, which would come to be known as the Sunflower Movement because student protestors used the flower as a symbol of hope, was led by [g0v](https://g0v.tw/en-US/&sa=D&ust=1552496400343000), a “civic hacker” group which saw the movement as an opportunity to promote transparency and the use of digital tools in the lawmaking process.[1] g0v had been working on improving the delivery of Taiwan’s public services since the group’s founding in 2012. Its first project, for instance, was a visualization [tool](http://budget.g0v.tw/budget) to help citizens understand how the national budget was allocated across sectors and at the local level. The tool was eventually adopted by Taipei’s Mayor to publish online visualizations of the city’s budget.

Jaclyn Tsai, Minister without Portfolio of the Executive Yuan (Taiwan’s parliament), was receptive to the group’s goal of promoting citizen engagement. At a g0v hackathon in December 2014, she asked the attendees if they could “create a platform for rational discussion and deliberation of policy issues that the entire nation could participate in.” In response to the Minister’s challenge, a team of g0v programmers headed by Audrey Tang and Chia-Liang “CL” Kao developed [vTaiwan](https://vtaiwan.tw/&sa=D&ust=1552496400344000), an open consultation process that brings together experts, government officials, and citizens on a national scale to deliberate, reach consensus, and craft legislation.[2]

**The Collective Intelligence Process**

*How it Works*

The vTaiwan lawmaking process has four key engagement stages: Proposal, Opinion, Reflection, and Ratification.

1. Proposal Stage

1. Every Wednesday, vTaiwan hosts a mini-hackathon where programmers, developers, public servants, journalists, scholars, legal specialists, students and others gather convene online or offline to propose issues to discuss. Anyone can propose an issue to a “competent government authority” who may choose to either accept (thereby becoming accountable for the issue) or refuse to take on the topic of the proposal. A proposed issue will not initiate the vTaiwan process without a government authority agreeing to become accountable for it, and a facilitator taking charge of the issue.
2. At each stage, the facilitator leads the group in a discussion about the issue. The vTaiwan community, meanwhile, is responsible for[[\]]](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ypAB2eX3EO8If7ycjmcDvibnd-jWtptTgtK55AnFysI/edit#bookmark=id.3dy6vkm)researching and identifying relevant stakeholders, defined as any person or group affected by and/or has knowledge about the given issue.
3. Tools - during the proposal stage, notes taken during mini hackathons are shared using the collaborative notetaking tool [HackMD](https://vtw.link/), while documents and presentations are shared using [SlideShare](https://www.slideshare.net/&sa=D&ust=1552496400348000).

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/bd5acf79-3b30-4eee-8515-c13ca52ed895.png)Figure 1: Screenshot of Slideshare, the tool used to share presentations and documents in the proposal stage.* [*https://www.slideshare.net/vtaiwan?utm\_campaign=profiletracking&utm\_medium=sssite&utm\_source=ssslideview*](https://www.slideshare.net/vtaiwan?utm_campaign=profiletracking&utm_medium=sssite&utm_source=ssslideview)

1. Opinion Stage

1. The vTaiwan community launches the opinion collection process and produces a description of the case in an easily-digestible form, including publishing any documents or research relevant to the proposal. Opinions are then gathered through “Rolling Questionnaires,” where stakeholders within the community’s network are sent questionnaires which ask what they know about the issue and their experiences with it. Stakeholders are also asked if they can recommend others with knowledge and/or experience relevant to the issue.
2. The vTaiwan community creates an online forum on which anyone, not restricted to Taiwan residents, can ask questions, comment on ideas or choose to “agree,” “disagree” or “pass” on others’ ideas, and that forum is open for a designated period of time. Each round of opinion collection lasts for at least one month, but there is no limit to the number of rounds.
3. Two digital platforms are then used to build consensus among participants.
4. [Discourse](https://www.discourse.org/&sa=D&ust=1552496400349000) is a discussion platform which allows users to tag competent authorities, who, in turn, are obliged to respond to comments within seven days.
5. is is an opinion mapping tool to help a large group build consensus by helping the group to visualize its own opinions. Participants develop a series of statements about the problem, which users can respond to by voting to ‘Agree,’ ‘Disagree’ or ‘Pass’ on those statements or answer “Is This Statement Important to You.” As users respond, the software develops an opinion landscape which visualizes in real time where this is consensus and where there is disagreement. At the end of the process, vTaiwan publishes reports on the results that are viewable by the public and submitted to the relevant government authority.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/6ef5fc0b-25d0-4681-a72b-e317adf961ed.png)Figure 2: Screenshot of the Pol.is tool user interface used for opinion mapping.*

[*https://pol.is/3phdex2kjf*](https://pol.is/3phdex2kjf)

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/cb25b071-f0cc-40aa-b73d-1a0ef4fd4fc0.png)Figure 3: Sample opinion map generated by the Pol.is tool.*

[*https://pol.is/3phdex2kjf*](https://pol.is/3phdex2kjf)

1. Reflection

1. Through two face-to-face events, the community reflects on the findings and decides if it is time to proceed. If so, they design an in-person consultation including identifying the size and scope of the issue.
2. At the consultation meeting, led by the facilitator, key stakeholders including scholars, public servants, private sector representatives, and participants who were deemed highly active during the earlier stages are invited to present on the issue at hand.  During this process, the facilitator takes notes digitally to document a summary in real-time, which is all displayed on the projector. Following the meeting, the videos are released on the vTaiwan Facebook page so that citizens can continue to share ideas in the following weeks.

3. Ratification

1. After the consultation, a final discussion on the results of the process which decides the action that the government will take. Considering the feedback that has been produced so far, including input from the relevant government agency, the community reaches a final resolution on the issue. The final outcomes can take one of two forms:

1. In some cases, the issue is resolved with a guideline, policy, or statement from the competent government agency. This often includes a point-by-point explanation of why legislation is not being enacted.
2. In others, the issue is formulated into a draft bill to be sent to the [Legislative Yuan](https://www.ly.gov.tw/EngPages/List.aspx?nodeid%3D345&sa=D&ust=1552496400353000) (Taiwanese Legislature).

The process is flexible and adaptive according to the unique challenges each issue presents. Rather than defining a threshold of support that each proposal must reach, the vTaiwan community decides to advance the proposal to the next stage when a “rough consensus” has been reached.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/fc50656b-8a15-46d7-99c4-5811f29bd5bc.png)Figure 4: Diagram of the vTaiwan Process* [*https://info.vtaiwan.tw/*](https://info.vtaiwan.tw/)

*Who Participates?*

Anyone can join any stage of the process. Participation is self-selected. A notable exception is the in-person consultation, which occurs during the Reflection stage, where attendees must be invited. Though, anyone can view the online livestream and contribute ideas through the chat, which the facilitator can decide to include in the meeting.

As g0v is the largest civic tech organization in Taiwan, the community has a substantial network for outreach. As g0v activist Wu Min Hsuan remarked in 2017, “I wouldn’t say that everyone knows g0v, but people who are interested in tech and/or in politics definitely do.”[3] For instance, during the Opinion stage, stakeholders within g0v’s network receive surveys to collect their feedback on the initial portions of the process from stakeholders. Surveys also reach others via online advertisements and Facebook.

vTaiwan has created a community that encourages open collaboration and experimentation, which in turn leads to sustained participation. This means that new participants do not have to start from a blank slate, Audrey Tang, Taiwan’s Digital Minister remarks that participants do not “...have to fight an existing authority \[and established\] culture that says no.”[4] For example, in the 2015 engagement about the regulation of Uber, there was active participation:

- 31,115 total votes (highest of any process to date)
- 145 statements submitted on Polis survey (during opinion gathering stage)
- 925 participants voted on Polis survey (opinion stage)
- 1,875 participants joined online during the two-hour live-streamed consultation meeting
- 4,000+ participants crowdsourced the meeting agenda for the consultation

*How is it run?*

g0v volunteers manage the process. The use of effective online tools has greatly diminished the need for human moderators. On the Pol.is platform, users “vote” on the comments of others rather than replying to them directly, which reduces the risk of “flame wars” and endless arguments. This functionality helps to drive the discussion and build consensus without the need for moderators.[5]

The unique, volunteer-based structure of vTaiwan also keeps costs down. Most of the tools used by vTaiwan are free. Pol.is is free to use and also open source. The vTaiwan process was supported pro bono by the organization that develops and maintains Pol.is, which provides support at negotiable fees. While g0v does not charge for its services, the value of having a team of tech-savvy civic hackers actively involved in the project should not be underestimated. The process also receives support from the Digital Ministry, which spends about $100,000 on the project.

**Key Innovations**

Taiwan’s Digital Minister, Audrey Tang, describes vTaiwan’s approach as a kind of “bootstrapping”-- a term borrowed from computing which means that the community uses its past work to drive itself forward rather than relying on external inputs. As Minister Tang said,**“I think \[vTaiwan\] is closer to the civic tech community than it is actually to my office or any minister...what we’re doing is institutionalizing the parts that worked.”** This approach is reflected in the plethora of related projects vTaiwan and the larger g0v community has developed to fill the gaps that vTaiwan is not designed to address.

A prime example is the online platform [Join](https://join.gov.tw/), launched in 2015. Join provides several functions --many of them inspired by previous projects-- on a common site that is maintained by Taiwan’s government. The petitioning function, like vTaiwan, uses Pol.is for consensus building. The forum section, where users can respond to petitions, uses and upvote/downvote functionality inspired by [Your Priorities](https://yrpri.org/domain/3) (the online forum software developed by the Citizens Foundation for the [Better Reykjavik](https://congress.crowd.law/case-better-reykjavik.html) initiative in Iceland). Another section, an adaptation of g0v’s inaugural project, visualizes the allocation of Taiwan’s national budget.

The vTaiwan community has also tackled democratic issues outside of lawmaking. In the run-up to each national election, the [vote.ly.g0v.tw](https://vote.ly.g0v.tw/) platform aggregates information about legislative candidates into a common system. This includes information such as the attendance and voting records of incumbent legislators on particular issues (e.g. education or finance) so that any user can easily compare candidates. Another example is [Fact Check 2020](https://www.readr.tw/project/fact-check-2020), a platform created to fact-check statements made by 2020 presidential candidates during campaign speeches and debates.

**Outcome and Impact**

To date, 200,000 people have participated on vTaiwan to define the problem around such complex issues as Uber, telemedicine, online alcohol sales and other hard topics. More than 80 percent of processes initiated on the platform have led to  “decisive government action”, including the passage of 26 pieces of national legislation.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/d732fbbe-7c44-4050-84dc-b0fdfa9c873b.png)Figure 5: Commenting and forming opinion groups using Pol.is* [*https://civichall.org/civicist/vtaiwan-democracy-frontier/*](https://civichall.org/civicist/vtaiwan-democracy-frontier/)

vTaiwan’s most impactful contribution has not been the sheer volume of participation nor its numerous legislative accomplishments, but the smoothing of public discourse around controversial issues. This is a result of the platform’s approach of bringing together groups with differing viewpoints to find a rough consensus. The 2015 debate over rideshare regulation, for example, engaged representatives from Uber Inc., the Association of Taxi Drivers in Taipei, Taiwan Taxi, and the Ministries of Transport and Communications, Economic Affairs, and Finance to create amendments to  the country’s existing regulations that were acceptable to all parties involved. This validated vTaiwan’s approach as a methodology for improving the quality of legislation even when dealing with a contentious topic.[6]

In 2016, a similar controversy about online sales of alcohol was partially resolved on the platform. In this instance, alcohol merchants, e-commerce platforms, and social groups had reached an impasse in a debate on how to regulate a 2011 law that legalized online sales of alcohol, which some feared would make it easier for children to surreptitiously purchase alcohol using the Internet. Over the course of several weeks, 450 citizens proposed and debated solutions to the issue on vTaiwan. Several of the resulting regulations --e.g. requiring the vendor to verify the age of the purchaser for online sales-- were incorporated into a series of amendments in a draft bill that were introduced to parliament in April of 2016. However, the bill did not pass parliament after President Tsai “withdrew all bills awaiting legislative approval” upon taking office in May of the same year. [7]

The flexibility of the vTaiwan process has also allowed the platform to experiment with new approaches to regulation. In 2017, a vTaiwan-initiated law created Taiwan’s first “regulatory sandbox”, which liberalized regulation for qualifying financial technology companies testing innovative approaches.[8] Similar regulatory sandboxes for electric scooter usage, autonomous vehicles, and the 5G spectrum network are currently in development on vTaiwan.

Join also plays a major role in resolving controversial debates on regulatory topics beyond the digital economy. In one recent example, a user posted a petition entitled [“](https://join.gov.tw/idea/detail/09ae5b7b-b8d9-4c92-bc51-46416f4b2df4)[Stop the Divine Pig Weight Competition Sacrifice](https://join.gov.tw/idea/detail/09ae5b7b-b8d9-4c92-bc51-46416f4b2df4)”, which called for an end to the practice of raising excessively fattened pigs for slaughter as part of the annual Hakka Yimin folk culture festival. Upon acquiring the requisite 5,000 signatures on Join, the case was adopted by three Participation Officers, who convened a series of collaborative meetings involving religious and cultural groups, animal rights groups, pig farmers, and relevant ministries.[9] These meetings produced a series of [recommendations](https://join.gov.tw/idea/detail/09ae5b7b-b8d9-4c92-bc51-46416f4b2df4) on how to resolve the dispute, which included:

- Recognizing the religious freedom of the Hakka people and the cultural significance of the divine pig sacrifice
- Encouraging Hakkas to transform the custom into a creative competition, where practitioners would craft holy pigs out of natural materials rather than slaughtering live animals
- Coaching by the Agricultural Committee to educate pig farmers about how to raise their animals in a more humane way

Divine pigs aside, the Participation Officer network has processed 60 such cases since its creation in 2017. The Join platform as a whole has seen more than 10 million unique visitors --nearly half of Taiwan’s population-- since its launch in 2015.[10] Minister Tang attributes this success in part to the platform’s innovative recommendation system. When a user clicks on a particular petition, for instance, the platform recommends related petitions, budgets, or regulations to comment on. This encourages users to keep participating as the platform retains their interest, similar to browsing products on Amazon or titles on Netflix.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/0ff007f0-0ce7-4e20-bff6-1bada688a3e2.png)Figure 6: Tracking the progress of a Join petition (translated by Google)*

[*https://join.gov.tw/idea/detail/09ae5b7b-b8d9-4c92-bc51-46416f4b2df4*](https://join.gov.tw/idea/detail/09ae5b7b-b8d9-4c92-bc51-46416f4b2df4)

**Current Status**

vTaiwan’s independence has helped the platform to achieve legitimacy in the eyes of its community and among members of parliament.  **Indeed, vTaiwan survived the transition from Ma Ying-jeou to Tsai in May of 2016, largely because the platform is seen as an independent, pro-transparency force that could benefit the opposition party as much as the incumbent administration.**

In recent years, the platform has become more closely tied to the government. In 2016 Audrey Tang, a key figure in the Sunflower Movement who led the development of vTaiwan and the Join platform, was appointed Digital Minister by President Tsai. Further, since 2017 a regulation has been in place that requires each ministry to appoint one or more “Participation Officers” (PO) to act as “links between the general public and the public sectors, and as channels for inter-agency collaboration”, which includes engaging in vTaiwan.

The creation of the PO network is a step toward mitigating one of the key risks of vTaiwan-- namely, that the appointment of Minister Tang, with her close ties to the platform, could make vTaiwan a target for a future leader seeking to undo the accomplishments of the Tsai Administration. “As long as there is a horizontal minister willing to call up relevant stakeholders within the government, which is easy now with the PO network, then the binding process is still there,” said Minister Tang. “My main function is just to ensure that the right stakeholders within the government show up.”

Yet, in the absence of a legal framework, the risk that a future administration could dismantle the binding power that vTaiwan currently enjoys remains a real possibility. The vTaiwan community has also made some attempts to institutionalize the process in law. One piece of legislation, a clause in the Digital Communications Acts (DCA), would have created a legal framework for the executive branch to respond to cross-ministerial issues that originated on forums like vTaiwan. However, this legislation, itself a product of vTaiwan, did not complete its parliamentary process in 2019 due to a technicality. President Tsai Ing-wen had previously promised to create a digital ministry or council to act as the competent authority for digital lawmaking. As the language in the DCA charged the president’s cabinet with this task rather than a designated ministry or council, the clause was considered outdated and did not pass.

Regardless, there appears to be cross-partisan support to create a dedicated authority to institutionalize digital policymaking processes like vTaiwan. During Taiwan’s 2020 presidential election President Tsai’s challenger, Han Kuo-yu, concurred with the need to create a dedicated authority rather than leaving the Cabinet to deal with digital lawmaking.

**Lessons Learned**

Due to its complexity and adaptation to the circumstances of Taiwan’s political system, it would be neither easy nor advisable to attempt a carbon copy of vTaiwan in another context. Despite lacking binding power by law, vTaiwan has achieved a high level of institutionalization through a unique combination of top-down political support and a grassroots ethos that lends the initiative legitimacy.

- **Administrative Buy-In:** Since its inception, vTaiwan has had a complicated relationship with Taiwan’s government. The platform was born out of a challenge from the Prime Minister, though one whose hand was forced by an anti-government protest movement. Despite this, the vTaiwan community has made a concerted effort to involve in response to the country’s civil servants not only in voting on legislation but also in its creation. While the involvement of Participation Officers on the Join platform is an obvious example, an even more high-profile instance is the vTaiwan-inspired [Presidential Hackathon](https://presidential-hackathon.taiwan.gov.tw/en/international-track/), the first of which was held in 2018. Through this event, teams use open data published by the country’s government to define public problems and propose solutions in a competition overseen and judged by the President herself, with the opportunity to develop these solutions in coordination with the government. Such involvement is crucial for public servants to see the value of supporting public engagement initiatives as a process that can provide valuable solutions rather than as simply a box to tick. Equally important is the process’s role in demonstrating that without some form of binding power, whether through legislation or administrative support, the collective intelligence of participants will not be reflected in the government’s actions.
- **Apolitical Approach:** From the beginning, vTaiwan intentionally insulated itself from affiliation with political parties. This is partly informed by g0v’s ethos. While the group considered forming a political party, g0v decided against it as not to become exclusionary. Pragmatically this approach has helped the initiative to avoid being tied to one particular administration. Beyond that, it has also helped to build a broad coalition of support among participants; it is not uncommon for vTaiwan meetings to have participants from five or more political parties. Public servants, too, see vTaiwan as a tool that can provide them benefits rather than a disruptive force that will threaten the power of their political party. “We see many collective intelligence tools have this...idea to take apart existing representative mechanisms. That will face a lot of headwind if a new administration or a new mayor comes” said Audrey Tang.

**CORRECTION**

An earlier version of this case study had an incorrect description of the cost structure for using [Pol.is](http://pol.is/). That information has been updated with the input of Pol.is. \[Updated October 20, 2020\]

# Belgian Sortition Models

**Institutionalizing deliberative democracy**

- Category: Level of Institutionalization
- Topic: Citizens’ Assemblies for Legislation
- Location: Ostbelgien Region, Belgium; Brussels-Capital Region, Belgium
- Owner: Parliament of the German-Speaking Community of Belgium (PDG); Parliament of the Brussels Region and Parliament of the French-Speaking Community (Cocof)
- Years in operation: 2019 - present
- Platforms: In-person deliberation; online petitioning, buergerdialog.be
- Project website: https://www.buergerdialog.be/ ; http://constitutionnet.org/news/belgiums-experiment-permanent-forms-deliberative-democracy
- Case study last updated: October 2020
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

In Belgium, two regional governments are trialling related, but distinct, models of deliberative democracy based on sortition -- the ancient practice of randomly selecting citizens to participate in legislative citizen assemblies.[1] While the parliament of the German-speaking Ostbelgien region, which has a population of only 77,000, was the first to adopt the sortition model in early 2019, the much larger Parliament of the Brussels-Capital Region, which has a population of 1.2 million, will implement their own sortition method in 2020. A selection of legislative committees, each comprising 17 legislators, will be complemented by a random sample of 45 citizens who will work alongside them.

These regional parliaments benefit from Belgium's unique federal system, which devolves substantial powers to the governments of each linguistic and cultural region. As political scientist Min Reuchamps writes, “Belgian Regions are critical actors as they oversee urban development and housing, environment, water and nature conservation, economy and employment policy, transport, public works, energy policy, local authorities and subsidiary authorities, external relations as well as scientific research.”[2] While it is too soon to report any impacts of these assemblies, **the adoption of these innovative methods -- the first of their kind to be institutionalized into formal lawmaking practice in the world --  will test whether the time-consuming sortition process can effectively use the collective intelligence of a randomly-selected group of citizens to set the legislative agenda and develop policy recommendations at a regional level.**

***The Ostbelgien Model***

The Ostbelgien (“East Belgian”) Model, launched in 2019, uses two randomly-selected citizen councils (one with 24 members to collaborate in setting the legislative agenda and one with 25 to 50 members to develop policy recommendations) who sit within the German-Speaking Parliament (PDG). Participants deliberate in-person at the parliament building in Eupen, the capital of the region of East Belgium. The G1000, a civil society organization, designed the model in collaboration with the PDG in 2018.

**How It All Started**

Belgium’s German-Speaking Parliament (PDG) first used a sortion-based citizens’ dialogue to debate the issue of childcare in September of 2017. The parliament randomly selected 26 East Belgians to gather in the city of Eupen to develop a “citizens’ agenda” of the most important issues within childcare and to participate in several days of workshops with experts to formulate policy recommendations. At the end of the process, the committee presented its agenda to members of parliament, who in turn [incorporated](https://www.ostbelgienfamilie.be/desktopdefault.aspx/tabid-5929/10113_read-54919/) the citizens’ recommendations into the so-called masterplan for childcare in East Belgium.[3]

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/f902f946-6e7b-4ba6-b0b3-d330a17b4ee3.png)Figure 1: Citizens presenting their agenda at during the 2017 trial in Ostbelgien (Source:* [*https://epale.ec.europa.eu/en/node/42418*](https://epale.ec.europa.eu/en/node/42418) */* [*CC BY 4.0*](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcode)*)*

Inspired by the experience and the enthusiasm of its participants, Alexander Miesen, President of the PDG, approached author and deliberative democracy advocate David Van Reybrouck with an idea: creating a permanent sortition method that would institutionalize the process within the region’s parliament.[4] In 2018, the G1000, Van Reybrouck’s organization for democratic innovation, brought together half a dozen experts, including the leaders of past sortition experiments in Ireland, Australia, and Poland along with several notable Belgian academics, to develop a model for implementing sortition in the PDG.

The output, which the G1000 branded the Ostbelgien Model, combines temporary agenda setting Citizens’ Councils with permanent Citizens’ Assemblies charged with making policy recommendations to the Parliament. The G1000 then worked with the PDG’s legal department to mold their model into a draft decree (the equivalent of a bill).

The German-Speaking Parliament unanimously adopted the [decree](https://www.buergerdialog.be/fileadmin/redakteure/downloads/Buergerdialog-Dekret.pdf) in February of 2019.[5]  The PDG launched the first Bürgerdialog (“Citizens’ Dialogue”) in September of 2019.

**The Collective Intelligence Process**

*How It Works*

To facilitate the Citizens’ Dialogue, the Ostbelgien Model created two new types of bodies with rotating membership within the PDG:  the Citizens’ Council and Citizens’ Assemblies.

The **Citizens’ Council** is the 24-person standing body in charge of selecting the topics that each citizens’ dialogue will cover, as well as determining the size of each Citizens’ Assembly. The Citizens’ Council comprises former Citizen Assembly participants, randomly selected by the Permanent Secretariat (a PDG employee in charge of facilitating the sortition process).[6] The PDG replaces one-third of the Citizen Council members with new participants every six months.

A **Citizens’ Assembly** is convened for each new topic selected by the Citizen Council. Each Assembly can have between 25 and 50 members, determined by the Citizen Council. Participants can be any willing member of the public selected through sortition by the Permanent Secretariat.

These bodies carry out the Citizens’ Dialogue process through four steps: Topic Selection, Deliberation, Policy Recommendations, and Implementation.

Once per year, the Citizens’ Council initiates a call for topic proposals. Any East Belgian, including members of the public, government, and Citizen Council members themselves can submit a topic for consideration using a form on the burgerdialog.be website, via email, or on paper. The Citizens’ Council can choose any topic so long as it has collected at least 100 signatures of support as falls within the power of the PDG.

The Citizens’ Council determines the size and life span for each Citizens’ Assembly, which is then convened by the Permanent Secretary. To prepare the participants, the Permanent Secretary provides the new Citizens’ Assembly with relevant information, invites experts to deliver presentations on the topic at hand, and selects an external moderator to lead the discussion.

Once the discussions have finished, the Citizens’ Assembly formulates a set of policy recommendations, which they discuss at an open meeting of the relevant parliamentary committee. The members of parliament and relevant minister then determine whether or not they want to implement the recommendations, and announce their decision at another open meeting. If the MP’s want to proceed, they can introduce the measures necessary for implementing the recommendations. If not, they must provide the Assembly with a detailed justification of why they have rejected their suggestions.

The Citizens’ Council and Permanent Secretary are in charge of monitoring the implementation of recommendations. Within one year, members of parliament, the relevant minister, and the Citizens’ Assembly members must hold another open meeting to discuss the progress Parliament has made in implementing the recommendations.

*Who Participates?*

Anyone aged 16 years or older who resides in one of the nine German-speaking municipalities in East Belgium is eligible to be randomly selected for a Citizens’ Assembly, so long as they do not hold public office. To smooth the learning curve, only those who previously participated in a Citizens’ Assembly are eligible for selection in the Citizens’ Council. The Permanent Secretary randomly selects participants through a sortition process overseen by a judge. If selected, participation is voluntary. The PDG covers participants’ travel costs and provides €64 per meeting as compensation for their time.

**Current Status**

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/c1591400-1a66-45c1-bccc-57a51cb417c2.png)Figure 2: The First Citizens’ Council in Ostbelgien (Source:* [*https://www.buergerdialog.be/news/detail/erster-buergerrat-hat-seine-arbeit-aufgenommen*](https://www.buergerdialog.be/news/detail/erster-buergerrat-hat-seine-arbeit-aufgenommen) */ ©PDG/CK)*

The PDG organized the first sortition process in July of 2019. As there has not yet any former Citizens’ Assembly members to choose from, the PDG randomly selected 1,000 residents who they invited to participate in the first Citizens’ Council. Of the 115 who replied positively, the PDG selected a random sample of 12, representative of the population with regard to age, gender, place of residence, and level of education. An additional six participants from the 2017 childcare sortition experiment and six representatives from political parties rounded out the group of 24.[7] The group met in Eupen in September and again in October to plan the topic selection process.

The Citizens’ Council organized the first call for proposals on October 1st. The Council asked residents to submit an idea for a topic including a title, explanation, and a reason why the topic is suitable for the citizens' assembly by October 31st. Each proposal then had until November 21 to gather the requisite 100 signatures, either on paper or through the burgerdialog.be [website](https://www.buergerdialog.be/).[8] The Council shortlisted the 13 best proposals and posted them for public comment on the website. After another meeting, the Council decided to convene the first Citizens’ Assembly on the topic of nursing staff and the care they provide to patients, posing the question: “Care concerns us all! How can the care conditions for staff and those affected be improved?”[9]

As of February 2020, the PDG is selecting the 25 Citizen Assembly participants who will develop policy proposals for the dialogue on nursing care. The PDG expects the first meetings to take place in March and early April of 2020.

Each year, the Citizens’ Council will approve a budget for the Citizen Dialogue process which the Parliament’s presidium must approve. These public funds cover the Permanent Secretary, compensation for the citizens who take part in the Citizens' Council, organizational and logistical costs, and fees of the experts and external moderator. While the exact cost will vary depending on the size and scope of each year’s meetings, the PDG estimates that the Citizen Dialogue will need a budget of € 140,000 per year.[10]

Though the German-Speaking Parliament passed the Citizens’ Dialogue decree in February of 2019, they decided to pause its implementation until June so as not to allow the country's general elections to influence the initiative.

<table width="624"><tbody><tr><td width="624"><p><em>Sortition: An Innovative Yet Ancient Practice</em></p><p>Sortition dates back to the democracy of ancient Athens, where in the fifth century BC, Cleisthenes instituted governance by lot. In ancient Athens, where democracy began, citizen competence and expertise were central to economic and military success. Athens developed extraordinary institutional innovations for governance— with and by citizens—of a population of a quarter million people spread across twenty-five hundred square kilometers. In doing so, it made it possible to aggregate and distribute knowledge across the realm. All in all, there were fourteen unique Athenian governing institutions that managed the polis, all comprising amateur citizen participants, not professionals. The city’s success, coupled with its openness and opportunity, attracted talented people from across the Mediterranean who helped populate these new institutions. In addition, every free adult male participated in the deliberations on the Pnyx, the hill west of the Acropolis.<sup>11</sup></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p>Today governments are bringing back the practice as a means of tapping the collective intelligence of citizens. Legislative bodies often use these randomly-selected groups, sometimes called “mini-publics”, for one-off reforms and to create an opportunity for engagement that is more informed, thoughtful and deliberative than a referendum (alone). Ireland, for instance, initiated a Constitutional Convention in 2012, in which 66 randomly-selected citizens and 33 politicians recommended changes to the country’s constitution. The convention recommended legalizing same-sex marriage, which a public referendum passed into law in 2015. Likewise, in 2017 an even larger Citizens' Assembly recommended amending the country’s constitution to legalize abortion, which again passed into law through a public referendum the next year.<sup>12</sup></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><em><img src="https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/82c34146-b96d-4ecf-9c23-714d7dad0863.png" alt="" width="1280" height="853">Figure 3: Dublin Castle, the site of the first meeting of the Irish Constitutional Convention</em></p><p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_Castle#/media/File:The_Dubhlinn_Gardens_Dublin_Castle_01.JPG"><em>https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_Castle#/media/File:The_Dubhlinn_Gardens_Dublin_Castle_01.JPG</em></a></p><p><a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/legalcode"><em>CC BY-SA 3.0</em></a></p><p><strong>&nbsp;</strong></p></td></tr></tbody></table>

The Ostbelgien Model, which Constitutional Convention organizer Dr. David Farrell helped to design, improves on the Irish experience in several ways. First, the PDG compensates participants for their time, which will help retain participants and increase the diversity of participation. Second, the Ostbelgien Model gives citizens rather than members of parliament the agenda-setting power. And most importantly, the Citizen Council rather than parliament holds the power to convene a Citizen Assembly. These changes demonstrate that Belgium is learning from the experience of others while continuing to improve the ancient practice of sortition. **“****Most things that exist in Ostbelgien exist elsewhere,” said Dr. Yves Dejaeghere, director of the G1000. “What we did is institutionalize it.”[13]**

***The Brussels Model***

The Parliament of the Brussels-Capital Region, led by a political coalition headed by the Green Party, will implement sortition in 2020. Later this year, the French-speaking parliament, which comprises the 72 members of the Regional Parliament who represent French-speaking districts, will also implement the same model. Unlike the Ostbelgien Model, the Brussels Model retains agenda-setting power in the hands of the parliament and creates a citizen assembly of 45 citizens who will serve on a parliamentary committee together with 17 legislators and make recommendations.

**How It All Started**

Even before the German-Speaking Parliament launched the Ostbelgien Model, Belgium’s Green Party supported the idea of including randomly selected citizens in parliamentary debates, but lacked the political support to implement it. Upon winning a number of new seats in the 2019 general elections, the Greens were able to include this democratic reform on the agenda for the new governing coalition.

The coalition thus drafted a bill that would allow a mixed committee of members of parliament and randomly selected citizens to draft policy recommendations for parliament to consider. President of the French-Speaking Parliament, Magali Plovie, shared that the goal of citizens’ committees was to create better relations between politicians and the people by giving the broader public a chance to participate in important debates about the future.[14]

In December of 2019, the Parliament of the Brussels Region passed the coalition’s proposal into law. Members of Parliament widely supported the measure: 60 MP’s voted in favor and the remaining 25 MP’s who were present abstained. The French-Speaking Parliament in Brussels (Cocof) also approved the bill.

**The Collective Intelligence Process**

*How It Works*

Once per year, the Regional Parliament and the Cocof can create one or more citizen assemblies comprising a random sample of residents who work with legislators to draft policy recommendations for a given topic. These assemblies are composed of 45 randomly selected citizens in the Regional Parliament and 36 in the Cocof. They are joined to the relevant standing committee for the topic at hand (15 legislators in the Regional Parliament and 12 in the Cocof).

Unlike in East Belgium, the Brussels Regional Parliament and Cocof do not give these citizen assemblies agenda-setting power. Rather, citizens propose ideas and the Bureau of the Parliament selects the topic and defines the task of each assembly. Any citizen can organize a petition, and any group of 100 citizens can post a petition on the Parliament’s [website](http://www.parlement.brussels/texte-de-la-declaration-de-politique-generale-du-gouvernement-bruxellois/). At least 1,000 citizens must sign the petition for the Parliament to consider choosing the topic. The topic must also fall within the competence of the Parliament to be considered.

After selecting the assembly members, the Parliament then organizes a series of meetings in which the citizen participants and MP’s deliberate on the topic and develop policy recommendations. The assembly lasts for a minimum of four days. The exact duration of the assembly depends on the topic and is determined by a scientific committee, composed of experts on participatory democracy, thematic experts, and members of the administration. At the end of deliberation, both citizen and parliamentary members of the assembly vote on each recommendation. Citizens vote secretly while the MP’s hold a public vote.

*![](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/d792a9af-ec60-42dd-899e-82c4b95a6368.jpg)Figure 4: Inside the Cocof. Photo courtesy of the French-speaking Parliament.*

If a majority of the citizens in the assembly approve a recommendation, those MP’s who voted against it or abstained must publicly justify their decision. Within six months, the standing committee shall publish a report justifying the steps they have taken toward addressing the recommendations. It must provide detailed reasons for its choice of follow-up actions. The standing committee invites the citizen participants to participate in a meeting where the committee presents the results of the report. As in the Ostbelgien Model, the Parliament is not bound by law to implement any of the recommendations that citizen assemblies make.[15]

*Who Participates?*

The Parliament chooses the participants for the citizen assemblies through two rounds of sortition. In the first round, the Parliament, working with the federal administration in charge of the national register, chooses random members of the public and invites them to participate. To be chosen one must be a resident of the Brussels Region who is at least 16 years old and not hold public office.  A second draw among those who have expressed interest in participating selects a sample that is representative of the gender, age, geography, level of education and language spoken of the region’s population. Citizens serve for the length of the assembly, which differs depending on the topic.

**Current Status**

The Parliament plans to hold the first citizen assemblies by the end of 2020. As the initiative passed so recently, they are still organizing and ironing out the details, but plan to start with two to three assemblies per year -- each one affiliated with a different parliamentary committee-- and then expand and repeat the process if it appears to be working.

The Parliament plans to use an online platform to explain the random selection process and track the process of each assembly. They do not plan to incorporate much use of technology beyond that in order to ensure that those who live in poverty can participate. This is based on the as-yet-to-be-tested assumption that face-to-face participation is more equitable than online participation. “Collective intelligence is more a question of diversity than interest,” said Jonathan Moskovic, Democratic Innovation Adviser for the Cocof. “What we really want --otherwise it will be a failure-- is we want to avoid having the usual suspects of participation.”[16] To reach less-represented populations, they will organize a campaign to make the public aware that will include traditional outreach through newspapers and radio as well as with unions and other non-governmental stakeholders.

The Parliament is also considering several steps to build its institutional capacity, including hiring a Permanent Secretary to administrate the process. They will also hire a scientific committee to evaluate the process and recommend improvements.

To ready participants, the Parliament is considering training, particularly language training for those who do not speak French or Flemish. They are also considering training MP’s to help them learn to support citizens and their ideas.

**Lessons for Institutionalization**

1. **Media Support Critical for Innovation:** Yves Dejaeghere and Jonathan Moskovic shared that for both the Ostbelgien Model and Brussels Model, media attention was important for getting the bill through parliament. While politicians may be wary of giving up their own power, it is very difficult for politicians to oppose measures that empower citizens without losing political support. “It is very hard as a politician to be against citizens,” said Dr. Dejaeghere. “So if you design something really well, but you still leave a handbrake for the Parliament itself...and have some media coming up, it is very hard for a politician to go against this.”  Indeed, neither bill received a single vote in opposition.
2. **Be Open to Experimentation:** Both models allow the flexibility for parliament to try out different approaches, as their backing legislation does not provide specific time spans for implementation or limit the topics that can be covered beyond what is legally necessary. Dr. Dejaeghere mentioned that while the media attention was helpful in getting the needed votes, it also puts a lot of pressure on the PDG to make the sortition approach works. “You must allow room for things to possibly go a bit wrong because you still have Parliament as a brake,” he told us. “So when I talk to politicians who do this for the first time, I always say first try something small, as an experiment.” Likewise, Jonathan Moskovic emphasized that implementing the Brussels Model will be a learning experience: **“We know that democracy --although most people don't think so-- is something that is in a constant and permanent evolution. So, of course, we'll learn by doing.”**
3. **Game-Changing Innovation or Toothless Tiger? You Won’t Know Until You Test It:** As no legislation has yet been passed through either model, it is difficult to predict what the impacts and outcomes of the citizen assemblies in Belgium will be. While it is possible that each will become a success story for the use of sortition and deliberative democracy, there are clear risks. First, the assumption that face-to-face participation is more equitable may prove to be wrong when residents complain of the costs associated with turning up somewhere in person. Second, if legislators choose to ignore citizen recommendations, this may lead to political conflict and dissatisfaction. Third, without adequate time and training, citizen recommendations may be illegal or impractical to implement. Perhaps the greatest risk of all is that the running of the mini-publics will be all sound and fury signifying nothing. “You could vote it out with a simple majority.” Dr. Dejaeghere said. “...A challenge with mini publics in general is that if they become toothless, then people agree it is not really worth the money to invest in them.”

# Creamos

**Co-creating youth-led social innovation projects in Chile**

- Category: CI How-to
- Topic: Open innovation, co-creation
- Location: Chile
- Implementation level: National
- Owner: INJUV (Instituto Nacional De La Juventud): National Youth Institute
- Years in operation: 2020 - present
- Platforms: CitizenLab
- Project website: https://www.injuv.gob.cl/creamos
- Case study last updated: 11/29/2022
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

This case study is part of a series on Youth Democracy. Click to find the others on [Nuortenbudjetti: Helsinki’s Youth Budget](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/nuortenbudjetti-helsinkis-youth-budget) and [Forum Jove BCN: Barcelona’s Youth Forum](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/forum-jove-bcn-barcelonas-youth-forum).

**Introduction**

Approximately 40% of Chile’s elderly population suffers from depression.[1] Nursing homes constantly face the challenge of being unable to provide adequate physical and mental stimulation for their elderly residents.[1] To address this unmet need, in 2021, Natalia Alfaro Pedrero, a 21-year old civil engineering student at the Universidad de la Frontera en Temuco, launched *Sembrando Sonrisas* (Sowing Smiles). The project focused on creating accessible wellness spaces–in the form of greenhouses–for elderly residents within two nursing homes in the Araucanía region of Chile. This project ensures that elderly people in these residences engage in physical activities like gardening, as well as social interactions that provide them with mental stimulation. *Sembrando Sonrisas* is one of 48 projects that have been executed by Chilean youth through participation in the program, *Creamos*.[2]

Established by [INJUV](https://www.injuv.gob.cl/) (Chile’s National Youth Institute) in 2020, [Creamos](https://creamos.injuv.cl/es-CL/) is an open innovation competition and co-creation program which empowers young people (ages 15-29) in Chile to design and implement social innovation projects in their communities. Each year, young people submit their ideas in response to an open call posted by INJUV via an online platform built upon [CitizenLab](https://www.citizenlab.co/?utm_term=citizen%20lab&utm_campaign=CitizenLab+EN-US+brand&utm_source=adwords&utm_medium=ppc&hsa_acc=1016526533&hsa_cam=16559961559&hsa_grp=133203714886&hsa_ad=587578239005&hsa_src=g&hsa_tgt=kwd-459103097684&hsa_kw=citizen%20lab&hsa_mt=p&hsa_net=adwords&hsa_ver=3&gclid=Cj0KCQjwvqeUBhCBARIsAOdt45YAbqldryM94EqoqRqBNRgLd_6yvWiiWbg-I6lZ3_H3SeC64JguWjMaAqybEALw_wcB), a community engagement platform designed for local governments. INJUV provides training, mentorship, funding and support for winning projects, allowing young people to turn their ideas into reality.

![Creamos](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/8d7d9718-c2b4-413f-9b50-fb1c9542621a.png)

Fig 1: A photo of the Creamos logo. [3]

According to program manager Mr. Benjamin Prado, Creamos was created to engage youth in community development The goal of the program is to combine youth participation, and leadership, within an interactive platform, that in turn facilitates the implementation of young people’s ideas.

**How Does It Work?**

Creamos is a year-long, annual program that consists of five stages:

**1\. Application/Idea Submission:** Applications to join the Creamos program are made through the [Citizen Participation Platform](http://creamos.injuv.cl/).[2] In Spring of each year (Autumn in the southern hemisphere), potential participants  submit their ideas for social change projects through an online application.[5] For the year 2022, this process runs from mid-March to mid-May. The platform then encourages submitees to comment on, debate, and vote on the ideas that have been generated.[6] In addition to submitting their ideas, applicants are required to provide biographical information about themselves, including their motivations for participating in Creamos.INJUV then evaluates each proposal based on three criteria (project relevance, their value proposition, and the motivations of each applicant)— in order to choose the participants who will advance to the next stage.[4] INJUV also takes the socio-economic standing of applicants into consideration when selecting applicants for its mentorship program, i.e. those from at-risk neighborhoods are given additional priority. In addition, proposals with high peer engagement (i.e. comments and votes) and which include a video, gain additional points during the selection process.Although only selected applicants are able to benefit from the program’s funding opportunities, all applicants, selected and not, gain access to Creamos’ online leadership courses. [7]

**2\. Training and Consulting:**  In this stage, young people who have been selected to participate in Creamos are invited to join a leadership training program to help develop their ideas into implementable social change projects.[2] In 2022, the Training and Consulting phase runs from early June to mid-August 2022.[6]

The training program involves:[7]

- ***Online training courses and webinars*** about topics such as Management of Social Projects, Information Technology, Human Rights, Socio-Environmental Challenges, and Leadership for Social Innovation.

- ***Specialized Mentoring:***  Local leaders or experts in areas related to each participant’s ideas are assigned to the participants as mentors. INJUV assists participants in locating these leaders and experts, and also provides methodological and logistical support regarding mentorship-related activities.

- ***Virtual Regional Meetings:*** Eight weekend sessions are curated, totaling 16 hours. These sessions support Creamos participants in their analysis of challenges within their communities.[7]

**3\. Implementation of Youth Advocacy Projects:** After completing the training program, Creamos participants are then eligible to apply for funding from INJUV. Funding provides a crucial step in turning their projects from ideas into realities. The funding application/implementation phase for 2022 will run from mid-August to the end of November.

Prior to completing the financing phase, INJUV evaluates suggested projects in terms of their impact, feasibility and prospective results. Upon conclusion of this evaluation, INJUV finances at least 30 projects that have been developed for implementation in areas across Chile. There is a 2 million pesos cap—approximately $2,300 USD— on financing support per project.

**4.  Evaluation and Closing:** After several months, INJUV reaches out to Creamos participants who have had their projects implemented in order to evaluate each project’s outcome, gain insights into the participants' experiences, and see how INJUV can help participants continue to be successful youth leaders.[3] For the year 2022, this follow-up will take place in December.

**Who Participates?**

The Creamos initiative targets Chileans ages 15-29. According to the project organizers, it is their understanding that this specific  population tends to be most interested in facilitating positive change within their communities. “They like to make themselves visible,” Mr. Prado told us. [4]

To reach the target population and encourage young people to participate in the program, INJUV makes use of social media advertisements, webinars, and emails.

As of 2022 there are over 41,000 people registered on the Creamos platform.[8] Approximately 27, 000 of those who are registered on the platform are young people—aged 15-29 years old.[4] People outside of this age range (e.g. relatives of people submitting ideas) can register for the platform but are not eligible to participate in the Creamos program.

Among registered users, 61% of Creamos’ participants are female, 36% are male, 2% are of an unspecified gender, and 1% did not indicate a gender.[6]

The number of individuals selected to participate in the program changes yearly, as it is dependent on the amount of resources allotted to the program each year. In the year of the program’s creation, 2020, Creamos selected 327 individuals to participate in the training program. In 2021 the program hosted 300 participants, and in 2022, 450 applicants are expected to be selected as beneficiaries of the Creamos program.

**Outcomes and Impacts**

As of 2022, INJUV has trained over 600 young people in social innovation and leadership skills through the Creamos program. Following this training, 48 projects have been executed across Chile.[2] The proposals that were developed through Creamos encompassed a variety of topics, but many popular topics touch upon areas highlighted by the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as education,  climate change and sustainability.

An example of a popular idea that has been developed through Creamos is “Formación sexual integral para adolecentes” (meaning “Comprehensive sexual education for adolescents” in English). This idea calls for the creation of workshops for women about sexual and reproductive health. Another example of a popular idea that has been developed through Creamos is “¡Voy Contigo!” (“I am with you”). This idea focused on developing a  volunteer network to give a helping hand to elderly people in Chile. [7]

Mr. Benjamin Prado, Program Manager of Creamos, notes that ”the main impact  of Creamos is the opportunity of empowering young people.” [4] The Creamos program has empowered young people to implement social impact projects within their communities.[4] Mr. Prado also notes that Creamos has “improved youth civic engagement in Chile.” [4] This is because INJUV has been able to use the Creamos platform to actively engage with young people, and incentivize this engagement by providing them with mentorship and resources that they need to solve problems within their communities.

**Challenges**

In an interview with Mr. Benjamin Pradohe highlighted a number of challenges that INJUV has encountered in facilitating the Creamos program:

- **Changes in Administration:** Because Creamos is overseen by INJUV—a government agency which falls under the federal Ministry of Social Development— changes in the Chilean government administration have a tendency to affect ideas and plans to improve or expand Creamos. For instance, Chile’s recent election of new president, Gabriel Boric, will likely influence the upcoming growth of Creamos, as any plans for Creamos in the near future would have to align with the Boric and his administration's  policies and agendas.

- **Organizational Challenges:**  According to Mr. Prado, ”INJUV has a lot of organizational challenges.” [4] These challenges are linked to the institute’s inability to effectively consolidate its new program structures and provide consistent or progressive financial resources to its programs each year. As an example, each year, Creamos only accepts a number of participants based on the financial resources allocated to the platform within each given year. In response to this, Mr. Prado points out that the Creamos program is now taking steps to “consolidate its methodologies, and understand how participation and activities are relevant, consistent, and can lead to a proven outcome.”  [4]

- **Short Implementation Timeline:** Within Creamos’ yearly process, the implementation stage runs for 3 months. At this stage, participants are required to report back with data about their accomplishments during the program–in order to evaluate the program’s results by the end of each year, as part of a compulsory evaluation that each of Chile’s national programs undergo annually. The short implementation period for projects has caused Creamos’ participants to express concerns, and poses the risk of forfeiting long term impact evaluation.

**Lessons Learned**

- **Create Incentives, Attract and Sustain Participation:** Mr. Prado notes that Creamos is constantly in competition with other youth engagement opportunities in Chile, making it difficult to catch and maintain the attention of young people since “they live in a culture of immediacy.” [4] While Creamos experienced a high level of participation in its first year (likely bolstered by the overall increase in online participation during 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic), participation declined slightly in 2021. In the future, INJUV will be developing additional incentives to maintain and increase participation from year to year. For instance, they are considering providing certificates that young people who participate in the program could add to their resumes, with the idea that holding this credential could help make young people more competitive on the job market. They are also thinking about ways to incorporate the Creamos platform into additional youth engagement programs.[4] For other institutions that are looking to mimic Creamos’ success. This experience underscores the importance of building incentives into the design of youth engagement initiatives in order to sustain participation in the long-term.

**Empower Regional Teams:** INJUV operates 16 regional offices across Chile, with a central office that is headed by Mr. Prado. In the case of other youth institutes like INJUV–that are looking to recreate a similar platform to Creamos, as well as a regional framework – it would be helpful to take steps to empower each region to ensure that they operate optimally. In the case of INJUV the institute  is looking to “empower its regional teams within the platform, by providing them with resources that they need to better facilitate INJUV’s activities–such as Creamos–in their respective regions.” [4]

## End notes

# Forum Jove BCN: Barcelona’s Youth Forum

**Citizens’ assembly empowers Barcelona youth to develop recommendations for the city council**

- Category: CI How-to
- Topic: Citizens’ assembly
- Location: Barcelona, Spain
- Implementation level: city
- Owner: Barcelona City Council
- Years in operation: 2021 - present
- Platforms: In-person deliberation
- Project website: https://www.decidim.barcelona/processes/forumjoveBCN
- Case study last updated: 11/29/2022
- Part of: [Collective Intelligence Case Studies](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/)

**This case study is part of a series on Youth Democracy. Click to find the others on [Nuortenbudjetti: Helsinki’s Youth Budget](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/nuortenbudjetti-helsinkis-youth-budget) and [Creamos: Co-creating youth-led social innovation projects in Chile](https://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/creamos)**.

**Introduction**

In recent years, Barcelona has witnessed an increasing number of violent youth protests. Throughout the majority of these protests, there was a sense among Barcelonian youth that their city council had failed to set up initiatives that empowered them. In response to the general discontent among youth, the Barcelona City Council established *Forum Jove BCN,* a citizens’ assembly that allows young people in Barcelona to develop recommendations for the city council to address their needs within the city. One of these recommendations–that was recently approved by the city council–is Operació “Coneix els teus recursos” (Operation “Know your resources''). It involves providing young people with access to government-managed resources for personal development; increasing communication between young people and the city government; and optimizing the way that information is dispersed to the city’s younger residents.[1]

Launched in 2021, [Forum Jove BCN](https://www.decidim.barcelona/processes/forumjoveBCN?locale=es), (“BCN Youth Forum”in English, or “Foro Joven BCN” in Spanish), is a deliberative assembly of 99 young people, ages  16-29, who are charged with making recommendations to the Barcelona City Council regarding policies that impact young people in the city.[2] As the COVID-19 pandemic significantly impacted young people’s ability to find jobs, access housing, and emotional health support, the Barcelona City Council developed Foro Joven BCN to generate policies using the recommendations of those closest to these problems.

            ![Bcn2](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/52959b9d-3cd2-4b4e-bc75-3e2777ec1f19.jpg)

*Fig 1: FòrumJoveBCN participants discuss the framing questions for the deliberative assembly. Image Credit: Deliberativa*

The forum empowers young people to meaningfully participate in policymaking at the city level by identifying and discussing their needs. It also encourages them to develop solutions to these needs within the city of Barcelona.

**How Does it Work?**

Forum Jove is a deliberative assembly where members meet to debate and develop recommendations for the Barcelona City Council. The council, in turn, helps to inform youth policies within the city. In its first year, the City Council asked the assembly to respond to the question:

*“As a young person who lives in Barcelona, what would you need to carry out your life project?”*

The Forum Jove BCN involves five phases:

1. **Selection of Participants

   First, a city council staff member developed a sample of possible participants that was representative of the age, gender, and socio-economic backgrounds of Barcelona’s youth population. Then, using the city’s database of addresses, Barcelona civil servants sent letters to the selected young people, inviting them to participate in the assembly. In total, 99 young people were brought together to participate in the assembly, which lasted for 6 weekends.
   **
2.  **Agenda setting

   The first two weekends were used to establish a working agenda for the assembly. The assembly members brainstormed responses to the question *‘As a young person who lives in Barcelona, what would you need to carry out your life project?’[3]* They chose three themes to focus on: Education, Emancipation and Mental Health, which to them encompassed the major issues affecting young people living within the city of Barcelona. Following this, the assembly members articulated framing questions that would guide discussion and debate around each of the three themes.**
3. **Debate and proposal generation:**

   For the remaining four weekends, the 99 member assembly was split by lottery into three subgroups, each aligned with one theme, with approximately 30 participants in each group. Each group was tasked with deliberating and developing recommendations in response to their respective framing questions.

   For the group that worked on Education, their framing question was:

   *“How can the City Council offer a labor, emotional, academic and values guidance service in the educational stage and beyond? Sub-question: What ways can the City Council improve and offer to disseminate the services it offers to different age groups?”*

   As for the group that worked on Emancipation, their question was:

   *“How can the City Council train, accompany and help youth so that they can emancipate themselves, from the age of 27, despite socioeconomic limitations?”*

   Finally the group that worked on Mental Health, their framing question was:

   *“How can the City Council promote (raise awareness, motivate, normalize) and provide resources to help (in work groups, workshops...) the mental and emotional health of young people in all the Districts of Barcelona?”*

   The assembly developed 27 recommendations as a result of the debate phase. Each recommendation had to gain at least 70% support from the entire youth assembly, in order to make it to the list of recommendations that was sent to the Barcelona City Council for approval.[4]

4.  **Study of recommendations:**Following the deliberation phase, the assembly delivered 22 recommendations for study by the City Council (Five of the 27 recommendations were omitted as they did not achieve the 70% support threshold). Five of these recommendations pertained to Education, eight pertained to Emancipation, and the remaining nine pertained to Mental Health.[1] The City Council then evaluated the recommendations to determine whether their suggested actions were within the jurisdiction and scope of the City Council to implement.
5. ****Return:****

   In the “return” phase, the Barcelona City Council provided Forum Jove BCN participants with feedback on their recommendations and explained which they accepted and which they rejected.[3]

   The City Council rejected only two out of the 22 recommendations that were presented, one of which fell under the theme of Emancipation, and the other the theme of Mental Health. One of the rejected recommendations advocated that the Madrid City Council require companies that want to work for the City Council to reserve jobs for inexperienced and experienced young people. This recommendation was rejected by the Barcelona City Council because it suggested an action that could force companies to hire inexperienced employees, which is not allowed under the city’s current legal framework. The other rejected recommendation called on the Barcelona City Council to subsidize and expand the city’s public mental health system by incorporating a broader range of services and activities such as private professional consultations and alternative therapy services for young people. It was rejected as the city did not see this recommendation as viable in its original format, and did not have the budget to support the recommendation.

   The City Council used [Decidim](https://decidim.org/) - a digital platform developed in Barcelona to facilitate citizen participation - to publish the results of Forum Jove BCN’s recommendations. In addition, the Barcelona City Council worked with a consultant, [Deliberativa](https://deliberativa.org/en/) - a Spanish civil society organization which provides research, design, and training support for participatory democracy projects - throughout the process. The City Council also allocated funds from its budget to facilitate the process.

![Bcn1](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/48a04d68-b33b-4238-9f60-b33726a7b2ba.jpg)

*Fig 2: FòrumJoveBCN participants developed recommendations around three thematic areas: Education, Emancipation, and Mental Health. Image Credit: Deliberativa*

**Who Participates?**

99 young people within the ages of 16-29 years old participated in the assembly. These young people were selected through a sortition process whereby a city council staff member selects a representative sample of young people by lottery, from across the districts within the city of Barcelona. This sample took into account the age, gender and socioeconomic standings of the young people in these districts. During the sortition process, Deliverativa helped the Barcelona City Council to select sample criteria for members of the assembly, while City Council staff mailed the letters to participants and ensured that the final group was  a representative sample.

**Outcome and Impacts**

The City Council accepted (i.e. committed to implement as policies) 20 of the recommendations issued by the assembly. Fifteen of these recommendations were approved with some degree of modifications.[1] The 20 approved recommendations were then added to a final report that was presented to the mayor of Barcelona for further consideration and then implementation. The goal moving forward is to meet back in a year from now and track what stage of implementation has been reached.

An example of a recommendation that was accepted by the Barcelona City Council was “Fòrum Jove i habitatge” (“Youth and Housing Forum”in English), under the Emancipation theme. This recommendation encouraged the Barcelona City Council to hold a yearly forum for young people that would aid in detecting their housing needs and problems, while also allowing them to create proposals to solve them. The recommendation was welcomed since Barcelona already regularly holds a general housing and rehabilitation forum (known as the “Fòrum d’Habitatge i Rehabilitació de Barcelona \[FHAR\]).” The city council believed that this recommendation could be accommodated within the existing FHAR framework where professionals, and participants, gather ideas, and provide expert advice concerning alternatives to housing in the city.[1]

It is difficult to measure the initiative’s overall impact, as the Forum Jove BCN is a recently established youth citizen engagement initiative whose initial recommendations and policy outcomes have not yet come to fruition. However, the initiative has shown some positive strides that are worth acknowledging. According to Mr. Yago Bermejo Abati, Co-director of Deliberativa, the deliberative process of Forum Jove BCN “tries to give autonomy to the participants” regarding agenda setting. The process empowered participants to work neutrally in regard to decision making, and to develop recommendations that are rooted in the lived experiences and expertise of Barcelona’s youth.

**Lessons Learned**

- **Experiment with new models -** While governments, nonprofits, and advocacy groups have experimented with the citizens’ assembly model to convene deliberations around [climate change](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/dec/10/cop26-global-citizens-assembly-planned-to-address-climate-crisis), [corruption](https://congress.crowd.law/case-rahvakogu.html), [abortion](https://www.irishtimes.com/news/ireland/irish-news/citizens-assembly-is-an-example-to-the-world-says-chairwoman-1.3539370), and [road safety](http://collective-intelligence.thegovlab.org/case/sharing-the-roads-safely-cycling-citizens-jury), Forum Jove BCN is unique for its use of the deliberative assembly approach to amplify the voices of young people. The assembly model signaled to young people that the City Council is making an effort to prioritize the problems affecting them in society. This, in turn, may encourage more and better participation among the youth.

- **Have a clear strategy -** Having a clear strategy regarding how stages within a platform would progress is necessary to ensure that the process runs smoothly. As an example, in the case of Forum Jove BCN, the process of running the three groups of young people that addressed the problems of Education, Emancipation, and Mental Health, was a great challenge logistically. As Mr Bermejo Abati put it, “dividing an assembly in three blocks is like delivering three assemblies.” [4] So, developing a streamlined strategy that acknowledges context specific limitations is important to avoid future challenges regarding this kind of model. In addition, in terms of agenda setting, a bottom-up approach worked quite well with Forum Jove BCN, as it allowed assembly members themselves - rather than the legislature, executive, or interest groups - to select the topics to focus on.

**Diversify language offerings -** One challenge that Forum Jove BCN faced was a high dropout rate among assembly members who are immigrants. One possible reason for this trend is that these individuals - who were largely immigrants from Latin America - may have been more comfortable working with the Spanish language, rather than Catalan, which was the predominant language choice in the Forum Jove BCN deliberative assembly. As well, it should be noted that of the youth population in Barcelona, approximately 40% is comprised of immigrants.[4] Therefore, in the future, the deliberative assembly is looking to diversify its language offerings to encourage and retain the participation of diverse youth demographics.

## End notes

1. Ajuntament de Barcelona, “DOCUMENT DE RETORN FÒRUM JOVE,” February 17, 2022. [https://ajbcn-decidim-barcelona.s3.amazonaws.com/decidim-barcelona/uploads/decidim/attachment/file/13418/DocumentRetorn\_ForumJove.pdf](https://ajbcn-decidim-barcelona.s3.amazonaws.com/decidim-barcelona/uploads/decidim/attachment/file/13418/DocumentRetorn_ForumJove.pdf)

2\. It should be noted that the project is known as both “Forum Jove BCN” (in Catalan) and “Foro Joven BCN” (in Spanish). We use both terms interchangeably in this case study.

3. See [https://www.decidim.barcelona/processes/forumjoveBCN?locale=es](https://www.decidim.barcelona/processes/forumjoveBCN?locale=es)

4\. Interview with Mr. Yago Bermejo Abati, Co-director of Deliberativa
